SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Albert "Budd" Johnson
Tape One

Washington, D. C.
March 1975

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
You want me to sit where I am and speak?
Yeah, sounds good.
All right. So -- that volume is pretty good?
Yeah.

This is beautiful. Here it is March 5th, 1975, and I'm sitting here with my lifelong friend, Budd Johnson, and Budd, we're going to sit here and reminisce a little bit about you, and about me, and you tell me about some of the things about you that I don't know, and we hope we'll have this for posterity so young people in the future can hear about a great saxophone player like you, and what you said about yourself, what you said about some of the great people that you came up with, and some of the things that you accomplished, and Lord knows that's plenty.
First, Budd, I want you -- this is Budd Albert Johnson, is that the way you -- how your name is pronounced, Budd, how is it?
Well, Albert, J. Johnson, Senior. That is the correct title, now.
Albert J.
And my mother's oldest brother nicknamed me Budd, and because I used to love butterbeans. He

called me Butterbeans, so later on in the years, as I grew up, as a little fellow, and they cut it short for Budd. And that's how I got that nickname. So now I always say Albert B-u-d-d, Budd, Johnson, and Budd is my professional name.
Beautiful.
And it stuck with me ever since I can remember. Yes.
And you were born where, Budd?

I was born in Dallas, Texas, December 14th, 1910. You know, a funny thing, it isn't funny, my parents were out one night to some friends' and they left me and my brother at home. My brother was playing around with some matches, and the house caught on fire. And he had just -- he was four years old, and I was two years old, and he had just learned how to reach the latch on the door, screen door, and open it.
Oh boy!
And he got me out of the house. The house burned to the ground, completely.
How do you like that!
And he saved my life, you know. You know, we were always very close -- not because of that --
Sure.
-- but you know. This is how a kid four years old would be thinking. That's really something, to
So you were the second son of -- what's your Dad's name, Budd?
My Dad's name is Albert J. Johnson, same as mine.
Albert J. JOhnson, and your mother's name was --
My name was -- my Mother's name was Kate Estella Johnson. Her maiden name was Peak, her family name was Peak, P-e-a-k.
So you were their second child, because you had -- your brother was two years older.
Yes. Well, actually, there was a son before my brother Keg, but --
I see.
-- he died, you know, when he --
I see.
-- was maybe a year old, something, and we never -- we don't even know him. We never remembered him.
Sure.
Keg was next, then I came along next, and then my sister, of course, nine years later than me.
Sure, your sister's name is --
My sister's name is Ruth Kathleen.
Ah, Kathleen.
Yeah, Hickman, now. Because she's married. And I named her Kathleen. I gave her that nickname -- middle name, Kathleen. My father let me give her the middle name.
Hey, that's beautiful. Hey, let's tell them about your dad, just a little bit, Budd.
All right.
What did you say his name was? Albert?
Albert.
Albert.
My Dad.
Yeah.

My Dad was a very talented man, you might say self-educated man. He went no farther than the fifth grade in school, and I never did question him on how he learned so much about music, but my Dad was a very good trumpet player, and he played the piano also, and he had an offer once, he told me, when he was a young man -- well, I guess he might have been in his mid-teens -- to go with Al G. Fields' circus, and they offered him $12.00 a week, he said, and that was a whole lot of money back in those times, because that had to be like, you know, 1800 and something, you know what I mean?
Yeah, right!
And of course his mother, she refused
to let him go. That reminds me of another mother that refused to let somebody go.
I know that story.

Anyway, he had to turn it down, because she said, "No, you're going to stay here and work and help me pay some of these bills, and where I can keep my eye on you." And of course he was obedient, and he stayed home.
Later, when he got up into manhood, then he took his music abilities out on the Church. He was head of the choir, and he played the organ in church for a while, and he used to play at Sunday School.
What was the name of that church, Budd, do you remember?
New Hope Baptist Church.
New Hope Baptist Church.
My grandmother's name is on the cornerstone of that church right today.
That's beautiful.

And so he was always -- in fact, he encouraged both me and my brother to play music. It was a desire of his, so when I was about seven years old he gave me piano lessons, and one of his friends who lived in the neighborhood, named Mr. Walton, was the piano teacher.
And Mr. Walton used to come by the house like once or twice a week, and give me these piano lessons. Well, I was

doing pretty good, but really, it was -- I was really -- it was strictly by ear, because I mean I would see those notes and, you know, being seven years old, and this cat was sitting there, with his pencil in his hand, when I'd make a mistake he'd rap my knuckles.

So actually, my mind wasn't really on the notes, and he would say, "No! It doesn't go this way, it goes like this." And he would sit down and play the little thing, and I guess this was my early form of ear training, because I would listen and watch his fingers and memorize it, and then I would sit down there and do exactly what he did. But I really wasn't reading the music. You know, because my eyes was half full of water from -- with the tears, and things, you know, and I couldn't see it, everything was blurred.

But I was really developing an ear then, so I did go up into sheet music, and I don't know how in the world I did it. It was all on ear, but I did remember a few little things, you know, how to finger the C scale correctly, and all of that sort of thing, and a couple of little exercises that were pretty to me. And so I probably would have went on and become a kind of piano player, but, you know, then, all of the cats was on me, they were saying "Hey, man, you playing the piano?" Says, "You gone be a sissy." Because it seemed like all of the piano players around was kind of sweet, back in those days.
: Right.
You know. So I didn't want to do that, and then all like the cats was on me, so I put the piano down.
In the meantime, my father had bought my brother a trombone, you know, and he was studying the trombone.
: That's Keg.

Keg, Keg Johnson, yes. So I told my mother, I said, "I want to play drums," because there was a couple of drummers around, you know, like I had seen A. Godley G. Gottlieb with Alphonso Trent's orchestra, and then that was a very good drummer that went to school. He was my brother's age, maybe a little bit older, named John R. Davis, which was a terrific drummer, and there was another fine drummer named John Humphries, John Humphries used to play with Troy Floyd.
John R. Davis -- These are bands, : He's a Texas man.

Yeah, these are Texas musicians, all right in Dallas John R. Davis played with a guy named Fred Murphey, who was a great alto saxophone player, in fact, he was one of the greatest I'd ever heard. And so my mother took me downtown and bought me a set of drums, and I came home and I used to set those drums up in the house and rap the hell out of them.
In fact, I became quite good, and I played profes-

sionally for about five years, and I never will forget one day Alphonso Trent's band was in town. These guys were all sharp. They used to wear these beautiful hand-made silk shirts, and be sharp all the time. They worked all of the finest hotels --
Something like that one you've got on now.

-- in the south. They worked all of the finest hotels in the south, and they were making like a hundred and a quarter a week then. They were like the Duke Ellington of that time. I mean it was called Alphonso Trent and his Orchestra of Gold. And these guys really inspired us, and Godley used to flip his sticks and go on -- all the whole thing was sensational drumming at that time.

Well, I worked up to be one of the best drummers around, and in fact I was, you know, flipping sticks on the floor, catching them behind my back, and twirling them, and beating, and imitating these guys, and I would say maybe I was about number five. I was about the fifth best.

So I started taking my drum -- the snare drum -- buckle it on to me, to school when I was in elementary school. I think maybe by then I was in about the third grade. And I never will forget my teacher. She was a beautiful lady named Mrs. Bailey, and I used to play --
What was the name of this school,
Budd?
This was (Darrell) Elementary School.
In Dallas.

In Dallas, Texas. And I used to play for the kids to march out for lunch time, and play for them to march back in, on -- you know, on my own, and I would be making up my rhythms, hurrup de bup de bup de bing, bom, brrrrrr, you know, just playing, and so maybe about when I got to the fourth grade there -- by this time, now, okay- My brother Kei, and a dear friend of ours named Herman Batts, that played the banjo, another dear friend of ours named (Treservant) Simms, who played the bass sousaphone, and another friend by the name of Arthur Alexander played the alto and clarinet.

And gee, you know, the trumpet player, we called him Sap, because he was sort of a dumb cat, could really play. His last name was Wilson. He had a brother named Norris Wilson that played trombone, and you know, I've forgotten Sap's first name, but it may come to me --
Well everybody had a nickname in those days.

Yeah, it may come to me a little later on, but anyway, we had been getting together and rehearsing, and we had a pretty good little old band. We used to just sit around in each other's back yards and play, and whatnot, and so a lady by the name of Miss Puckett, she heard us, and she

came around to all of our parents' houses like in the summer time, and said, "Gee," she says, "I would like to chaperon the band and take them. You know, we would go around to Terrell, Texas, Wichita Falls, Texas, and the different little places, and play these dances. Can you imagine? At that age?

So anyway, we used to do that, and she wouldn't pay us till we got back to Dallas. Now this is going to kill you, because -- I have to laugh about it when I think about it. Every once in a while I think about these things. We would go out and play, she would pay for our food, and pay for our room, and get in the car, we'd go to the next little old town, all these little towns, and play these dances, and matinees, and in the day. We wasn't playing at night. They would be like matinees.

And when she says, "Okay, now, we'll all drive back to my house and I'll figure up what I owe you, and then you can get paid." Okay, so we would go to her house. She lived right on Hall Street, and she had --
I know where that is.
She had like one of these what we call shotgun houses. You could open the front door and look all the way through to the back door.
Anyway, Miss Puckett, Miss Puckett was a pretty hip lady, and she would have these young girls there, and she made home brew. So when we would come in there and all set around,

and she says, 'You want a little home brew, honey?' And we'd say, 'Yessum.' You know, and she'd give us a little glass of home brew, and hey, this is nice, you know? And the little chicks would be trying to make us, you know. At that age, well, what the hell, we were into a lot of things at that age.
Sure.

So, okay, she would call us in one at a time and settle the account, so when she got to me she called me in, and she said, 'Well now you know,' she said, 'The car had to move, and I spent so much and so much for your food, and room --' because what was room rent, like 25 cents?
Yeah.

Something like that, you know. And 'You had three home brews -- ' you know. And this chick, when she would get through, see, we made -- we'd gone out for a week and come back home, and she says, 'Okay, this would-be --' so you got 75 cents coming.'
Okay? You know, that was great. I had a ball. I'm traveling, seeing the world, so-called, you know, and so I would take the 75 cents.

Well, our parents -- our parents could trust us, because, you know, we come up in pretty good background, and we wouldn't do nothing too wrong that they -- you know. So anyway, this kept going on. The little band kept getting better
and better.

All right, by the time where I finished elementary school we had decided to enlarge the band -- oh, incidentally, the name of this band was The Moonlight Melody Six. We called it the Moonlight Melody Six.

So now, when we go into high school we have the same guys, but with a few more. We have augmented the band by this time now, I had taught Booker Pittman -- that's Booker T. Washington's grandson. I had taught him how to play the alto saxophone, because now I had been learning how to play the saxophone all this time, while playing the drums.

Incidentally, there was one number we used to call the 'Country Picnic,' and where I would get up and I would take each guy's horn and play a solo on it, like the trombone, the trumpet, and the saxophone, and whatnot, and then wind up back on the drums.
: On your drums.
Soloing.
: Hm! That's really fine.

MR. JOHNSON: So the only thing I could never play was the bass and the piano. But anyway, by this time we had augmented the band, and we changed the name of the band to the Blue Moon Chasers. And actually, this was a good band. Man, the two of us really began to start in the summer time, and I can remember just as well, on one of my first tours --

See, I -- we had been listening to every band that come into Dallas. We would go and hear them, and stand up in front of the band and just absorb all of the music we could, and we'd go back and try to imitate whatever good we thought was there, and incidentally, by the same token, we were copying records, like Red Nichols and HIIs Five Pennies; copying Coleman Hawkins solos off the record there; Fletcher Henderson, and some of Louie Armstrong, ~~we~~ he'd started recording for Okeh Records, and we would copy his -- solos.

We Would copy anybody's solo that was good, and I don't care whether it was a piano, or ~~want~~ you, know, we would try to copy this. Well actually, all of this was really a school, because, you know, you're copying off of a record, you're really developing an ear. It's -- and pitch, and you're learning how -- we wasn't writing it down, though. All of this would just play this over and over and over till we could hum the solos, and when we could hum the solos, then we would find it on our instruments, you see? And that's why they used to say anything you can hum, you ought to be able to play.

So anyway, we -- there was a band called the Southern Serenaders, from Tulsa, Oklahoma, and they had a drummer. His name was Ernest Williams. Ernest was a sharp little dude. He reminded me a lot of J. C. ~~Herd~~ Heard. You know, he was about that size, and he was just --
What was his name?
Ernest Williams. And he was very dap, you know, stayed clean and neat all the time, and he had a good gift of gab. And he aspired to become like a booking agent.

So he had heard about our band, because they all come to Dallas, and you know, sometime we would play a matinee before the night dance, and these cats would come up there and listen to us play. He told us one day, 'I got a job in Tulsa, Oklahoma, a road house, out on the outskirts of Tulsa, Oklahoma.'
A road house, that's -- road house. That's a place outside of town.
Yeah, because they weren't allowed -- this kind of thing wasn't allowed in the city --
In the city proper.
-- proper, because --
Get out on the highway.

That's right, because there was a lot of drinking, and you know, they usually put them in the woods. Before that I used to play with Red Calhoun in Dallas, Texas. He played a lot of clarinet. I was playing drums with him, and we used to play at a road house, black road house, in Dallas, Texas, in a place called Elm Thicket, and so these road houses were very popular. People could go out there and these -- this was back in the woods where -- way out. Nobody
couldn't distrub the peace, or anything.
Now we I-already know what a road house is.
Yeah.
Today.
Yeah, and it usually was off of a road that that's what they -- it's off of the beaten path.

So anyway, he says this job will pay $25.00 a week, and what? Oh, that's beautiful. That's a whole lot of money. So it was like in the summer, after school. We never did try to cut school, or anything, and everything took place like in the summer, on our vacation time. All our parents let us go. He had picked us up in his car, and drove us to Tulsa, Oklahoma.

When we got to the place we were supposed to play, there was a big padlock on the door. They had closed this place up for some reason. I don't know what, but here we are in Tulsa, Oklahoma now, nobody's got, you know, any money, and we're all stranded. So he drove us in to Tulsa proper, and got us some rooms at the Greenwood Hotel. That's on Greenwood and Archer Street in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and back-on, and we shared rooms like three and four to a room, because the man was just -- he was very nice, the owner, and he let -- he knew we were young kids, and he trusted us to pay him. He figured he could get his money.
So here we are, in these rooms, right? Now we have

to find some work. So in the meantime there was a theater down the street on Greenwood, and they used to have all of the TOBA shows to come in there. You know? And what is that, Theatrical Black ARTists? [Theater Owners Booking Association].
Yes, that's right.

TOBA? And of course this is the first time I ever met Pigmeat Markham. Pigmeat came there with a show called Gonzelle White. She played saxophone. She was very good, and they had a very good show, and this is where they had --
This is in Tulsa, right?

This is in Tulsa, Oklahoma. I guess this was -- this must have been about 1924. You know? About 1924. I'm 14 years old now, see, going on 14. So Harry Smith the trumpet player, great trumpet player that lived around Kansas City, was in this show, and Pigmeat Markham was the comedian in this show, and we went and persuaded the woman, people that owned the show, to let us ballyhoo out front, and that's bally up just before the show was going to start inside. We would get out there and blow, and attract attention, so that the people would look at the marquee, and would stand around and listen to us, and I would do a little barking, and tell them about the show inside.
And for this she gave the band $4.00 a day. So we would take that $4.00. Now we could eat, you see, and what-
ever else little money we had we would try to save it up so we could try to pay some rent.

Well anyway, summer was running out on us, and we haven't made enough money to pay the rent, so now we're planning on how to get back home. So we met a guy, they call him Lightnin', and he had a Packard sedan, Packard automobile, and we propositioned him, and he said yeah, he would drive us back to Dallas for $75.00.

Well we only had saved up about $25.00, so we wrote to our parents, you know, and they said they would give him the rest of the money when he came, so okay. Now we had to get out of this hotel. So we all had inside rooms, and there was a big chute that went all the way down to the floor, so we would stick our heads out, the cat on the top floor would drop his bag down. We'd catch it, and then the cat on the next floor, we'd drop it to him and he'd catch it, until we got all the --
This was like about 3:00 o'clock in the morning, and until we got all of the bags out and we snuck out of the hotel, got in the car, and we're gone.
Now I have been back to Tulsa many times, but that man never asked me for the money. You know? And he never asked anybody for the money, but however, we went on back to Dallas.
Okay, so I'm playing around Dallas, and we are all getting quite good, you know. We're getting quite good.
Keg is with you then.
Keg is with me all the way.
All the way.
We never did separate until we came to Kansas City, and I can tell you about that story later.
Sure, a little later on, or ahead, oh.
But anyway, we're playing --
Just before you go into this, Budd, I just want to establish the fact that your father used to work for Studebaker Wagon Company, didn't he?
My father worked with Studebaker when they made wagons, before they ever made cars.
Before they made cars.
And --
That's a quite interesting thing. I wanted to get that --
Oh yeah, well let me tell you something about that. My father worked for Studebaker before they ever made cars, and the --
They was big wagon makers. They made wagons!
Oh, they made the best wagons --
That went to the west. They went to the west.
They had a name for making the best
wagons in the country.
This is important, that people realize that the great wagon companies became automobile companies. They --

That is true. That is absolutely true, because I remember this, myself. And my father sometimes would drive the boss's car. He had an electric car. And I rode in the electric cars, back in those days. My father would come home for something and he would take me for a little spin and then would go on back to work.

Anyway, when they started making cars my father made that transition on his own by reading. He had all kind of civil engineer books, all kind of books that he read all the time, and he knew all about motors, and what not, and he became the first mechanic for the Studebaker plant in Dallas --
Isn't that beautiful?

-- and he was head of the parts department, hired and fired and he had, in fact, black and white people that worked. They all had to come through him. He got so good with the automobiles until he was the only man that would handle the Studebaker car at the automobile shows at the state fair. You know?
Which was a big deal.
It was a big deal, because me and my brother, he would have tickets. We could come in there because
they segregated when -- they had just a day for black people to come there.
Right. Juneteenth, usually.

All the other -- yeah, the 19th of June. And look, it was so segregated that you know that the Fourth of July was really the day for the Emancipation, but they wouldn't let the Negroes have Fourth of July, so they gave them the 19th of June.
19th of June.
Called it the Juneteenth.
Juneteenth.

Anyway, me and my brother were able to go there, because my father was the head man in there demonstrating the Studebaker automobile, and so we would go and watch the automobile races, and all of this sort of thing, and the old man got so good he could build the Studebakers up from the chassis. He could put it -- all that motor together and everything, from the chassis up.

He got so good till when the Depression hit they couldn't fire him. They didn't fire him. They didn't want to fire him, because he was like doing the job of three men, I guess, to keep his job, there handling all those departments in there, and this is one of the places I learned to drive, because like when some of the little towns didn't have railroads, and by Dallas having the Studebaker plant there they
would order cars and then they would have to be driven to these little towns.
So the old man would get me, he had taught me how to drive. He never taught my brother how to drive. Keg never did know how to drive.
Is that right? (Inaudible.)
I believe he could have driven a car, but I don't think he ever had a desire to want to drive an automobile.
Same with me. I have no desire.

I know you don't. And you and Keg was so much alike there. Anyway, I used to drive these cars to the little towns with my father, and whatnot, and we would work there sometimes in the summer when there was nothing doing with the horn, and would you believe it? We would be making like a a dollar and a quarter an hour. We would be unloading cars out of these box cars, you know, they would come in the freight cars and we would then beat that sheet metal loose with the big chisel and hammers, and then they'd work them on jacks and work them out of the car and put them in the plant.

And we made a plenty money doing that. I mean you had no idea, man. I used to make so much money doing that, you know, till I was started -- started neglecting my music, because then I could buy things.
Well, anyway, my father --
I just want to bring him in, yeah.

-- he was a great man, you know. He was the kind of man that if he saw two people fighting in the street he might go there to try to break it up. Of course I wouldn't suggest it nowadays, but then -- and he -- they would probably wind up, one of them would wind up in church with him next Sunday. And he was like that.

And sometimes he would do a little preaching in the church, they would let him preach, the old man. I was amazed, I was amazed at how he got all of this knowledge, and with no schooling, but he kept his head in books and newspapers and everything --
Determination, Budd, determination.

That's right. In fact, he got so good, and he knew a lot of big people in Dallas, I mean millionaires and whatnot, they told him to take the bar exam, that he could pass it, could be a lawyer. But he never did care for politics, and my father was always exempted from poll tax. He never paid any poll tax. He could vote, and he carried --
This was a rare thing for the black man in those days in Texas.
That's right, but he had to carry a little card, showing that he was exempted from poll tax, and all of that, because of influential people that he knew, and whatnot, you know.
In his association with Studebaker, Company.
That's right.
And a member of the Church. Did your mother sing in this choir?

No, my mother had a nice voice, but she sung every song that they -- you know, like doing the -- after Sunday school, see my brother and I we would go to Sunday School, and then my mother and father would come to the 11:00 o'clock service, then we had to come out of Sunday School and then go sit with our family. And then they would add a lot of singing, and my mother knew all of those sings. She could really sing beautiful, and -- but she never sang in the choir.

She -- I don't guess she had -- because they used to do a lot of rehearsing, and my father made all of those meetings, you know, like he was in church every other night, you know, with all of these different meetings, whatnot. And my Mama, mother then was -- she was strictly a housewife. She didn't do anything, you know. And -- until we grew up. So anyway, --
I'm glad to be sharing this interview with you, because you know, I knew your mother.
I knew you did.
And I used to stay -- when I used to
travel through Texas I used to stay with a dear friend of hers, Miss (Searcy.) Curley?
Oh, Miss (Searcy). They were real, real beautiful friends.
2312 Hugo Street.
That's right.
And Miss (Searcy) used to tell that --
I just want to interject this, not to take your story away from you.
Oh, beautiful! I know you did --
Because it's such a beautiful thing to know Mrs. Johnson. I used to call her --
Well you were like one of the family, like.
That's right.
You know, and because you and my brother was so --
Sure.
-- so tight. Okay.
(Phone rings.)
Just hold this up for the phone.
Right. [Pause] Are we rolling?
Yeah, Budd, we're still talking after the telephone call. And we just want to get back to (fooling) around Tulsa and Greenwood and you had -- you wanted
to bring something back up to (inaudible).
Oh yes, and I told you that our mothers had paid the rest of the money, and we came back to Dallas, and -- in this Packard car.
That was in 1924, something, you said.

Yes, '24 and '25, into that era. So we went back. We are talking about the band that I told you we had organized. I'm glad you stopped for a moment, because I seem to have lost that thing. Wait till we find it. It's in here.
Here it is.

All right. Yes, we went back, and of course we were back in school. We worked around, and actually, at that time we had on piano a great little man by the name of Charlie Durham. Charlie Durham was a great fullback on the highschool team. And he played beautiful piano. He had been working with us, and he was a little short guy, could do ten seconds flat, a hundred yards, in his football togs. He was a great little fullback.

And so Charlie had to leave the band, and we were auditioning piano players. So I just want to make one correction in John Chilton's Who's Who of Jazz, and where he mentioned that when I changed to tenor sax and played with local Blue Moon Chasers, and occasionally in a big band organized by

Sammy Price, in 1927, this is really not correct, although I know the dates and things get mixed up, but I would like to set the record straight right here with Milt Hinton. The Blue Moon Chasers, as I had said previously, was organized by our little school band, which had been going since the Moonlight Melody Six, and I said that when we went to high school we changed the name to the Blue Moon Chasers.
Right.

Now how Sammy Price came into the picture, it was like this. We were looking for a piano player. So Sammy Price was playing piano at that time, pretty good! Any way we played this club and Duke Ellington at that time was out there, and Orson Welles and all of them were behind him, and they were producing 'jump for joy.'
: Oh.

It had just opened, this great show, 'Jump for Joy.' And of course Ben Webster, being Ben, was hanging out every night, so a funny thing happened. Ben said 'how much you making a week, man?' Well, by this time -- oh, I'm a little ahead of myself. When we organized this band, we had to set up salaries, so we set up the salary for the men, at $7.00 a night. Bill Eckstein and myself were making $10.00 a night, and it was understood that -- Earl said you and Billie did this for me, you're going to make as much as money. You know, you cats will always make the same amount of money. And we were paying Earl $15.00 a night.
Now, mind you, Earl had nothing -- no control over the money. In the meantime now we have set Charlie Carpenter up in New York with William Morris' office. Charlie--
: Charlie Carpenter is now manager for George Kirby.
George Kirby, that's right.
: Chicago kid.
That's right.
: He was on some songwriting (inaudible).
"You Can Depend On Me."
"You Can Depend On Me."

And he wrote quite a few nice things which -- big tunes. He's in ASCAP behind that too. He made a lot of money off of that. Any way, we had Charlie up in the William Morris office by now, so that he could watch our route, because in those days if you didn't watch the and the jumps you had to make way you were travelling at the juncture there, the bus company would make all the money.
Right.
So we were trying to keep these jumps in order so that we could --
In line.
In line, so that we wouldn't be jumping all the way out here and all the way back to the East Coast to do a date, and then all the way down south to do a date.
Right.

We would plan our tour, and that's why we had Charlie up there. Well, in the meantime we were paying Earl $15.00 a night, and Billy Eckstein and myself were making $10.00 a night and we were paying the men seven. Now, we have saved so much money for Earl, so one night Earl came to us and says "okay, fellas, he says, look, $15.00 a night ain't enough for me, I'm the band leader, he says I got to have more money." So we said, okay, Earl -- see, he had to come before us

before he could do anything. And we handle all the business so we knew everything that was going on. So we said, okay then Earl, I mean, you'll get 20, I says, so -- and Billy Eckstein and myself, we'll make 15. We'll raise the guys to 10. Because we're doing pretty good now.

Okay. In the meantime we had set up a corporation for Earl Hines, and Earl was now worth more money than he had ever been in his life before because he never saved any of his money before and he couldn't get to this money. He had to come through us to get into any of this money.
Right.

So, okay, so we went on and we went on and we went on, so one day down in Hot Springs, Arkansas before we hit Billy Eckstein came to me, he said, okay, B, he says I just got my raise. You know, because we were supposed to make the same money. I said, yeah, how much you making now, he says Earl said I could make $25.00 a night. I said -- so he said 'you'd better go on down and get yours straight.' I said 'will do.' So I walked down into the dressing room and said okay, you raised Billy 25 a night, I want my 25 a night. He said 'I can't afford to pay you $25.00 a night, B,' and he says you know -- I said, 'Look Earl, don't tell me what you can't afford to pay, I'm looking at the books every night. I know every penny that comes in and what goes out,' I says, 'and you can afford to pay.'

He says, yeah, but Billy Eckstein is the star, he said -- I said, I wouldn't care who is the star. I said it was the agreement that Billy would make no more than me, I wouldn't make no more than Billy, and that we organized and founded the band, and I did all of the rehearsing, I'm writing the music and everything. I says, I don't care how big it is, I figure I'm entitled to the same money.
Right.

So he says, well man, I can't give it to you. I said, you can't give it to me, I said, okay, I'm quitting. So now this was in December of 1942 now. I jumped my story a little bit because I didn't bring in '41.
Yeah, go ahead, bring it in any time you want.

Any way, I'll go back to '41. So in '41 -- well after we got -- we were able to make some records in L.A. and get enough money for us to get back to Chicago, and this is when we recorded 'Jelly, Jelly, Jelly' and all those things like that, of course which is my arrangement too.
Is that so, that's your arrangement?
Yeah. And Billy Eckstein wrote the lyrics.
That's the all time record for him.
Yeah. And 'Boogie Woogie on the St. Louis Blues' is my arrangement too.
That's Earl's great solo.

That's Earl's great solo, you know. So we wrote -- I wrote all of this stuff, and we were able to make enough money to get out of California. In the meantime we were invited out by Nat King Cole to go hang out with him at a party, he was playing a party for some big people there in Hollywood, and then we went out and was drinking and eating and having a night with Nat King Cole. And this is when he was playing the piano, and he had just first really started to try to sing, you know. Evidently he had done it before but not maybe in public, you know, and so he was playing and singing and everything, and everything went beautifully and these people was talking about Nat King Cole, they were behind him 100 percent, and he did have a beautiful trio.
Prince French was the bass player?
Yeah and --
Oscar Moore was the guitar.
The guitar player, yeah.
Trio.

That's right. And I took my horn out and you know, for the cats we blew with them, what not, hung out. Because I knew Nat King Cole from Chicago. You remember when his brother and he organized a band, Eddie Cole left (Unintelligible) and came back to Chicago.
Right.

And they tried to organize a big band and just like you were saying King Cole was so raggedy that like be like (unintelligible). When he walked he would hum. He really was, like Milt said, he was really -- was scuffling.
(Inaudible) in Chicago.
They were really scuffling, and they did pretty nice, they did a pretty good little band there for a while. But I still say King Cole's singing style sort of came from Eddie. I think.
Eddie Cole.
Yeah, his brother.
His brother was always the one we always figured was the most likely to succeed.
He had nothing but talent.
Nothing but talent.
Yeah, that's right.
He played bass, he played piano, he sang and everything.

And later on when I was in Honolulu with Benny Goodman, well he had a television show, him and his wife. But any way, '41 we went back to California, and this time we went out there and we made some V disk -- no, I mean that's with Billy Eckstein -- I mean with Earl Hines. We went back to California. It wasn't quite as bad this time, and we had a pretty good little tour and then we came back and then

that was in the latter part of '41. And in '42 we toured all over until finally in December of '42 when I had this little confrontation with Earl about salary and everything, and he said he couldn't pay me, I says okay, if you can't pay me I'm leaving the band. So he said, well I can't pay you, B, I said okay, I said then you'll have to get somebody else, I'm leaving tonight. I'm going through Dallas and seeing my mother and then I'm going on back to New York because by this time my son had been born in September of '42 and I really wanted to get back home any way.

So John Williams then, he says, 'man, you're responsible for me coming into the band,' he says, don't go. He said 'don't go, I'll give you part of my salary to stay.' I said, 'I couldn't do that, John, you deserve even that and more.' I said I feel that I'm doing it, it's a moral thing with me, and it's a matter of like, you know, the way it should go down. And I said, I mean, you know, I'm going to go on back to New York.

So that night they bought me a pint of Canadian Club, and -- George Dixon and Billy and all of them, and put me on the bus and saw me off to Dallas. And I went and stayed with my mother a few days and I came on into New York. Well, now I'm in New York, and I'm going --
You come to New York alone.
I'm alone. And of course my wife was
in New York, she had an apartment and everything. And I had a few nickels --
This is your second wife now isn't it?

This is my second wife now, Bernice Johnson, who was a very great, great, great girl. And I started to getting out, I would like take me $5.00 and get out and get around and see who's doing what, what not. So I went up on 52nd Street and when I got to 52nd Street I went by a place called the Moon Glow.
This is 1942, right?

This is 1942. December of '42. And there was Dizzy Gillespie, Don Byas, Max Roach, Oscar Pettiford, and a little piano out there that Dizzy was trying to teach how to play the piano named George Wallington. George later wrote 'Lemon Drops', you know.
Really? For Woody Herman.

Woody Herman. But he couldn't play no more piano than me, and I can't play piano at all, you know. But Dizzy was very patient, he's a very patient man and he was schooling this little cat. Any way, I used to go by and sit in with the band, so Don Byas told me one night, he says, hey man, he says why don't you come on and take this job.
Can you hold that just a second, I hear a squeak?
All right.
Just a second. So what were you saying Budd?

As I said Don Byas asked me, said hey Budd, why don't you come on and take this job because I'm going to join Duke Ellington's orchestra. I said, oh, yeah, when? He says, well I can join it right away, he says, so why don't you just come on and take this job and I'll go on over there and you've got you a job while you're here. Well, you know, Don Byas -- Don Byas I had known since he was a little kid, because when I used to play down through Oklahoma he was from Muskogee, Oklahoma, and him and Hal Singer. And they used to come and stand in front of the band at the dances when I was down there with George E. Lee, and listen to me play, and all like that, you know. But -- and I knew him then, you know, when he was a kid. So he felt like, you know, he'd like to do something for me, you know, because I thought it was very beautiful. He said, so you take this job because I'm going to go with Duke.
Okay, so that night I stayed on after the show, after it was over, and we rehearsed. And then I started to work --
After what show?
Well, you know, we were playing at the Moonglow, which was a little night club, you know, on 22nd
Street.
You were playing with who there?
With Dizzy Gillespie. I mean, this is where I used to come by and sit in and while I'm sitting in Don said why don't you take this job.
Oh, I see.

So all right, that night I stayed on and rehearsed because he's not going to be there tomorrow night. I'm starting to work. So I run over the hits and everything, and they're showing me the different things, you know, and so I started to working with Dizzy Gillespie and Oscar Pettiford (inaudible).
Hold it just a second.
So that's when you started working with Dizzy and Pettiford Pennifort.

Yeah, and some of the tunes I had to learn, they were pretty difficult, I'm going to tell you, because this is in the bop thing. So we had heard Diz, you know, and everybody was very interested in the new music and so this is -- all due respect to what Dizzy did later on, Pettiford I mean I used to put down the melodies for Oscar Patty. He would say, 'hey Buddy, write this down, I've got a tune,' and these are the kind of tunes we were doing. And this -- what they call 'one base hit' Oscar wrote that tune and it was called for 'base faces on me.' And we were playing like Max 'Is Making Bass Only
"Wax", and we were playing like "Salt Peanuts", and we were playing like (Singing of notes) salt peanuts, salt peanuts, and we were playing like (singing of notes).
What is that, Be Bop?
Yes.
What's the name of that?
I can't think of the name of that.
But any way (Singing of notes). We were playing all these tunes, men, and like they were pretty difficult.
They're difficult today, Budd.
My yes.
These young kids are scuffing trying to play these things. It's beautiful.
It's really difficult, and you know, I happened to play that one day for Diz and he said "you still remember that?" So any way it was a good thing for me because I wanted to get into this.
Well, this was a new trend now, wasn't it?
A new trend.
This was where another trend started. This is 52nd Street and 42.
And you know, a lot of people they have different conceptions about how that name be bop came about, but from the way I see it and remember it, it came about because
like Dizzy would be trying to hum the way he wanted you to play, and like he would write a phrase and he'd say no, it doesn't go like that, it goes like (singing of notes), you know.
Yeah.

And this is the way he would explain the phrase to you, and this is the way I think the name be bop was born. Because the guy would say hey man, make play some more of that be bop music, and like because he was -- Dizzy would hum it.
He always hummed.
(Singing of notes). You know.
Yes.
And so I think it got its name that way, and that's because that's my own way of thinking, and I'm pretty sure.
Well, I don't know anybody who's more of an authority on it than you.
Well, I'm pretty sure that's really the way it came about, because -- but any way it was a great way of explaining it because then you could get the phrasing that he wanted.
How did you guys come to record this?
Well, one day, the first recording that I had a chance to make with this, Coleman Hawkins came

back and -- from Europe and Coleman -- which, you know, was always a friend of mine. I had known Coleman since about 1926. And Coleman -- well, we lived around the corner from eachother. He lived in a place called the King Haven on 151st Street, and I lived at 152nd Street between Convent and Amsterdam.
This was in New York?

This was in New York, and I used to go visit him, so he told me he says look, he says, I've got a record date coming up; I'm going to record, and he says "I want to know how all of these cats who's playing all of the new music, you know, he says, "because I'm going to pick up on what they're doing." And so he said--well at that time Clyde Hart --
Piano.

Piano player, who was -- I spoke of earlier, was the great arranger and everything. Clyde and I had been doing some writing together, and he says I want you to do something and I'm going to do some things. I want Dizzy to do something, you know,and we're going to make a record date. So okay, we made this record date and Hawkes, had Diz, Clyde Hart on piano, who else was on that date? I Played baritone sax. And any way I played on the date and I did this arrangement, Clyde Hart and myself (unintelligible) called By-ke-Dakt Vo-De-Dot. By-De-Dakt
Vo-De-Dot.
Yeah. See, that was the language of

be bop in those days, and Dizzy did "Woody is 'ya" Wouldn't You." He made that arrangement then, you know, and Hawk did this thing. He says, well, I'm going to record this thing, what did he call it, "Moon Mist" or something. He says, I'm going to record this over because it was my solo, "Body and Soul" that made this, and I own the solo, so I'm going to call it something else and record it over. So he recorded that and fixed up some things like that.
Howard McGhee was on the date too.
Howard --
Trumpet player.
Say, Budd, what I'm trying to find out is who were some of the guys that came around to get you all to make -- like the A and R man?
Oh, yeah.
Who were these guys who came out to 52nd Street to ask you that?

Well, you know, one of the cats -- I'll tell you two of the guys were -- okay, I'll have to connect this up because after the Moon Glow and I started to working over there -- I'll tie that up like this.
Sure.
After the Moonglow, Don Byas was supposed to go with Duke Ellington, I told you.
Yeah, right.
Well, it turned out that he didn't get with Duke Ellington, Al Sears had gotten the job.
Oh.

So he came back by and he told me this, I felt very bad. I said, well, hey man, can you take your job back, he said, no, you keep that job, I'm going to get another job. So in other words I stayed there and I worked and then after the Moon Glow closed Oscar Pettiford felt that he wanted to go get his own group and so Dizzy and I said okay we'll stick together. So I was the business manager and Dizzy Gillespie was the musical director, and we went across the street to the Yacht Club and took a group in there. And Oscar Pettiford kept a group in the Moon Glow. So I'm getting to your question.

All right, after we -- when we were in the Yacht Club then I think Lorraine was then interceding for Dizzy to go with William Morris, and any way he signed up with William Morris. But before he did you know the street was full of guys looking for recordings, you know, and of course one of the main guys was Timmy Rosenkrantz. You know, Timmy Rosenkrantz was a beautiful guy. He was actually royalty.
Yes, baron of something.
He was a real baron, but I mean he was something like the black sheep in his family.
European family.

Yeah, but they sent him his money like every month, and he would come off to America here and he would work at record stores and everything and be connected with recording companies. He used to come around. Teddy Riggs was beginning to get into it.
Ruth Records.
With Ruth Records. Well, this was with Savoy before Ruth.
I see.

And there was another record company called Deluxe Records, and all of these guys were like hustling up guys to record on -- from 52nd Street, because that's all -- Art Tatum, everybody used to come there. I remember one night Djang Reinhardt had just gotten into town and he couldn't even wait to get to his hotel room. He sent his bags onto the hotel room and he took his guitar and he broke out to 52nd Street and he came over to the "Three Deuces" and he just wanted to sit in and play with some American musicians. Of course he was highly efficient, he was a great guitarist and he just loved to play.

But anyway these guys used to come around and hustle up different groups to make records, and at that time they had hustled Hawk up to make this record. Hawk wanted to be associated -- he was crazy about Thelonious Monk, and to my recollection Monk had the first modern tunes alive. I mean, if
you wanted to play any modern music you played Monk's tune. That was before Dizzy.
He was hip.
Yeah. But any way Hawk got us all together to make this record, and it of course was one of the first bop recordings, you know, and --
You don't remember the tune, do you?
The one that I wrote was called De Dakt But
Oh, yes.

That was in the bop language, you know, (Singing of tunes), you know. Dizzy wrote Woody 'Ya' Wouldn't You (Singing of Notes), a beautiful number, right today I don't think there's no better writing than that.
By the way there was a lot of thievery going on, a lot of parties given, people had wire recordings.

You better believe it. These little old Webster wire recorders, and it would -- you know, actually it's a whole lot of stuff been kettled into the European countries. You might be sitting up you say hey, that sounds like me. And it was probably something you did at a party.
Right.
Well, in Europe you know they'll buy anything like somebody with some name on it, and they'll clean

it up and they'll just put out a certain amount of these things, maybe 1500 of them, collector's items. And people just to say like they have some Bird records when he was first here, had some of your records when you first did something, or -- and they can get these names --
And you didn't get a dime out of it.

We never got a dime out of it. I think maybe one day, but you know this is a very complicated thing. I'm just learning now that you have to belong to all of these different societies all over the world in order to collect.
Uh-huh.

But they have a little tighter thing. If there's anything you ever done in France or Germany or England, that money is still there waiting for you to just collect it if you join one of these societies. You know? And --
Most of us didn't know anything about it.
No, of course not. I mean, I was writing for writing's sake, you know, I was playing, just happy to be playing --
Sure.
-- with certain cats. And you know, we had a difficult enough time just trying to keep up with

what's going on and learning how to play your instrument rather than to try to be a businessman with a lawyer and all of that sort of thing. Because you know, that's what you're dealing with, you're dealing with cats that knows all about business administration, knows about law when you're talking to him. If he doesn't here's a guy sitting in his presence listening to what you say, he's a lawyer or something. So I mean, it's just a trickery thing.
Sure.
This business is all trickery, I mean it's fortunes been made off of us that we'll probably never get. Maybe --
There's a lot of thievery going on and we could call it that now.
That's what it is too.
Go around to 52nd Street, and all these parties, these chic people from the East Side, they invite you by --
Believe it.
-- (inaudible).
These cats get high and play their hearts out, and they would be taping all of this stuff down.
Sure.
There's a guy, I understand, Willie Randall knows him personally in Chicago, and I think he's a
professor of chemistry at Northwestern University. You went to Northwestern, didn't you?
Yes, yes.

Well, this guy is a chemist, and 21k he has catalogued every show that was on the air. He sells his stuff all over the world, and he's got it in chronological order in the years and the dates and the personnel he's collected and everything. I understand he's just probably making thousands and thousands and thousands of dollars.
He sure should. No royalties to pay to anybody.

He's probably too smart to sell it, he probably leases it out, you know, to these different record companies. Because, I mean, when I was with Billy Eckstein, later, which I haven't gotten to, but we made some V disk in California with the armed forces that was not supposed to be used for personal -- I mean commercial purposes whatsoever. I got -- well, I know a man in London, Doug Dobell Dougman who has the largest record shop in London, and we're very good friends and all of the guys work with him. I hear from him, in fact I got a letter today from one of the guys.

They sent me an album with the cover of our pictures on it and everything, and that V Disc. They sent that music, they sent it to me and I told Billy Eckstein about it, and you see what they do, they get ahold of this stuff and
they don't try to flood the market with it, they sell it at a higher price, and they might just put out 2000 of them.
They make it exclusive.

Make it exclusive, the collectors, you see. So he sent me this and was I surprised because it got out of the hands of the United States Government. Well, you know, since Nixon pulled it off, I mean, I can understand how things can lead. But it is so much thievery in this business, I mean, you know.
It was a great deal in those days, with you guys just --
Oh, man.
-- so happy to be playing with each-other.
Who knew anything about copyrighting material, I mean these guys came along the street and copyrighted all of that, practically all of that stuff. And you turn around and it's gone.
Right.

That was one pretty smart guy named Walter Fuller. Not the trumpet player but the arranger. He came walking through the street there and he was calling us fools to our face. He says, you don't do nothing but smoke and drink, you don't know what's going on, and he was stealing all of this stuff, setting himself up in business and every-
Sure.
And so any way it was so much of that going on it wasn't even funny.
How long did you hang around (Unintelligible) on the Street.

Well, I was on the Street until -- let's see, off and on I was on the Street until it closed. I would say the Street probably folded about 1944, you know, but any way what happened from the streets some nice things happened to me. They had a place right around the corner on Sixth Avenue off of 52nd Street called The White Rose. Well --
That was a great bar.

It was a great bar, and we used to -- these are some of the oldest bars in New York, and run by some pretty great guys, I think, I used to know. But any way, this -- I understand the original White Rose is still up there on 125th Street near Broadway. That is the first one I understand. But any way, I'm standing in there with Hawk, Coleman Hawkins, we called him Bean and everything, you know. The reason we called him Bean?
No, what is it?

Because he was so intelligent about music and the way he could play and the way he could think and the way his chord progressions run, we'd call him the Bean. Instead of Egghead, you know, we called him the Bean, you know.
Like Egghead, that's how he got that name.
(Unintelligible) with the head.
Yeah, the Bean. So any way --
He was a pretty good piano player wasn't he?

Oh, his whole family can play the piano, everybody plays the piano. You know a lot of things people don't know about Hawk. He never was too much to brag on himself, but Coleman Hawkins, I found, was -- went to the University of Kansas. And he was a music student at the University of Kansas.
Where was he from?
Hawk was from St. Joseph, Missouri.
Right.

That's where his family's from. And before he even joined Fletcher Henderson he had been to the University of Kansas, and you know, that's been a long time ago. And a funny thing about, Hawk didn't register in the first draft. I said come on Bean, how old are you, he never would reveal his true age.
(Inaudible).
But any way -- what was I trying to get to?
We were just talking about the street and how you -- you said some nice things happened to you
in the street.

Oh, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. The reason I brought up Coleman Hawkins' name, he and I were standing the White Rose drinking one night, so in walked Jerry Jerome who was a saxophone player, tenor saxophone player and clarinet.
Who was he playing with?

Well, he used to play with Benny Goodman. I'll go back and give you a little story. One day when Hamp came -- see Hamp, before he organized his band he wanted me to be the musical director for his band, and we were negotiating. So when Benny Goodman came to Chicago to play at the Chicago Theatre Hamp had a record date set up. So he had wired me ahead and asked me to make some arrangements with a record date, and Spencer Odom and myself wrote some arrangements for --
He was a pianist.

Was a pianist, yes. And very good arranger. And he was back in one of those Roy Nance groups, see and this boy had nothing but talent. And so we did and when Hamp came in town we were recording this music. we made Til Tom's Special and Toots Camarato was in the band. He wrote Shades of Jade, and we recorded a lot of stuff there.
What did Toots Camarato play?
Toots Camarato was a great first

alto saxophone man, and he played with Benny Goodman and now he's probably still working in the studios. I happened to run into him in the airport in Paris one day and he was on vacation. But here's a man that made a lot of money playing because he was a fine first alto saxophone player. And then of course he went into the studio, of course he was probably making $1,000.00 a week up to the studios for three years, and years and years. money for tools to make

Of course that was really no (unintelligible) as popular as he was in the many things he was. He probably was ace at the stockmarkets and you know, but any way. I always admired Toots. But any way we were recording, so I felt this man looking at me on my left, and he's looking and he finally said, 'Bud, you don't remember me, do you?' And I said 'tell you the truth, I really can't call you a name, you know, it's (unintelligible). He said, 'well my name is Jerry Jerome,' he says, 'you know, when I first met you you came -- I was going to the University of Alabama studying medicine, and you came there with Earl Hines' and he says 'you cats played so great and I talked with you and everything.' I said, oh, yeah so bla, bla, bla.

I went on to say that this was my first record with Jerome Jones. So when we're in the White Rose, he came in and he says Bud Johnson. I said, hey, J., what do you know, baby. Oh, fine, have a drink. I said, okay, don't care if I do. So we're drinking and he said something, meet my manager,

He introduced me to his manager, I forget his name. So he says what are you doing, I said, well I'm working around the corner on the street. He said, are you still writing those beautiful arrangements. I said, well I'm still writing, Jerry. He says, well let me tell you, I'm now a conductor for NBC, and he says, I certainly would like for you to write some music for me. I said, well, it would be a pleasure, he says okay meet me up to NBC tomorrow at 9:30 in the morning and we'll take you and see what we can do. He said I don't have a budget yet, like I can't tell you what I want to write, I mean what I want you to write, but we'll go up and get everything straight (unintelligible).

So I met him the next morning, at 9:30 up at NBC. A guy by the name of Mr. Bill Paisley was the librarian in charge of the library at that time. So they talked to me and signed me up to a contract. Now I'm a staff arranger at NBC. They signed me up to a contract --
What year was that, Budd?
Well, this was the latter part of '43.

Yeah, see. I'm a staff arranger at NBC now, and I'm commissioned to do four arrangements a week. Well, I didn't know when -- what I had to do but I always had a little heart that I would try anything one time. So when he called me then we sat down in a little conference room and he was typing out what he was going to do. I said, what's your
