And, you know, he was a great greeter. I don't think nobody could greet anybody any more beautiful than Louie Armstrong, even if he didn't know you. He made you feel that -- that you knew him.

So, he says, "Yeah, man, what's happenin' there?" He says, "We want to present you with this." And, they held their arms out like that, and it was a great big joint rolled in the form of a baseball bat. It must have been about a foot long. And, they had taken, like, a fountain pen and punched holes in it to read, "To the king of the vipers from the vipers club of St. Louis, Missouri."

And, you know, back in those days, it was not illegal to smoke pot. I mean, we -- we smoked pot all over the bandstand, and so, I asked Louie, I said, "Louie, what we gonna do with this, man?" He says, "We're gonna smoke a little bit of it every day, and then we're gonna have Mezz for dessert. Now, Mezz Mezzrow used to mail to Louie, through the mail every where we went, marijuana. And --
MR. : Milt Mezzrow.
Yeah.
MR. : Great clarinet player.

Yeah. Mezz, Mezz. So -- so, okay, we got smoking this joint. Now, when -- at intermission, when we're going to smoke, if we didn't have a dressing room, the police would stand in front of the bandstand so nobody could get to us while we -- while we got high. If we had a dressing room, we would all go in Louie's dressing room and then close the door and the police would put his chair right in front of the door and sit there so nobody could enter. And -- while we got high. Nobody never bothered us about getting high.

So, when we left -- we left St. Louis, we -- we played another dance in St. Louis before we left, and that was against the band called the Crackerjacks. And, Hal Baker was the trumpet player in the Crackerjacks. So, I never will forget. We took our intermission and just before we were
gonna get back on the stand, they played "Shine". And, he imitated Louie playing "Shine".

Well, this kind of upset Pops. He says, "Can you imagine that? What is he trying to do?" But, see, Hal Baker was hitting G's just above the staff -- in the first space above the staff and ended on a high C. Well, when they came off the stand, Louie says, "Shine." He called "Shine". And, man, I counted 'em. He hit 250 high C's and ended on a F -- a high F that you wouldn't believe. It just like rung the rafters in the place, man. In the -- like, because, he was saying, "Nobody's gonna --" You know. And, you know, the home town really clapping to hell.
But, when Louie went into that and hit those 250 high C's, baby, and that was the whole ball game.

Okay. So, we left out of there and we went to Oklahoma City. And, we played a dance there. Well, man, we had gotten blind, because Louie had turned us on with this mez, you know. And, so, we were all sitting up on the bandstand playing and, like, you know, all I could see was just images. I couldn't make out nobody's face, I was so high. But, I felt all right. But, I mean -- so, a lady walked up. She said, "My, my. They all look so tired and sleepy. But, the music is good."
And, she couldn't figure out what was going on, you know. Yeah.
I want to ask you a couple of things about some of the songs (unintelligible) when you mentioned "Shine".
Yeah.
Did he play "Beau Koo Jack" in those days?

"Beau Koo Jack", yeah, "Ding Dong Daddy", "Mahogany Hall Stomp", you know. All of those. And, he -- he used to play "Ding Dong Daddy" then like I've never heard. "Big Butter and Egg Man". And, of course, we played all of our recordings, "World on a String", and all that stuff. But, he would go back and get some of those old ones. We used to play "High Society". And, where all of the clarinets had to play that solo.
(Singing)
You know. And -- (Inaudible) ball systems then?

Oh, yes. We was playing band systems. I started out on Albert, though, you know. But -- in high school, the high school days. I played Albert. And, then, of course, when Boehm became popular, you know, and -- and everybody jumped to Boehm. But, all of the old masters like Buster Bailey and --
Burney Bigard
-- Barnaby Guard, and all of them, they still play Albert. Man, and I tried to -- I tried to play a
little bit of Albert, you know, lately, and that hung me, man. I said " (Inaudible) what?
I say, Herb Hall still plays -- Boehm
Herb Hall still plays the [Albert]
system, and --
Albert System.
And, so did -- what is the Albert that died over in Europe?
Nicholas Albert --
Albert Nicholas. He played Boehm Albert, too. Very few guys play that instrument.
That's right.
And, this -- this is great, because, I mean, they can really walk over it, man. Buster Bailey was just one of my favorites for clarinet players. And, if not the -- if not my favorite, you know.
Who were some of the good saxophone players around Chicago in that days, Budd?
Let me see now.
How about old Leon --
Leon Washington. Of course, I don't think I had met Leon at that time. But, then, you had Boyd Atkins.
Boyd Atkins, yes, sir.
Boyd Atkins -- Boyd Atkins was a
band leader, too.
That's right. I worked for him.
Yeah. He was one of those guys that had the band in the theaters there in Chicago.
Right.

Boyd Atkins -- of course, you know Omar Simson and Darnell played a lot of clarinet and violin. Of course, they were with Earl. I hadn't -- I used to hear them all the time, but I hadn't joined the band at that time. And, Cecil Irving played very good tenor. And --
I want -- I wanted to ask you about the Doll, the trumpet player --
Oh, Doll! Doll Hutchison.
Yeah. And, her husband was a --
Yeah.
Was he tenor player? (inaudible)?
What did Doll's husband play?
I think he played tenor.
I believe so.
And (inaudible).
And, oh! What is the guy? Washington that used to play with Louie. Dark fellow. I think he's a school teacher. He was -- turned out to be a school teacher. Not Leon Washington.
: Al Washington?
Another Washington.
: Jack Washington, was it?
No, Jack Washington played with Basie's.
: That's right.
Well, anyway, Scoops Carey was playing. He was really the Charlie Parker of his time.
: That's right.
Scoops played the tremendous amount of alto saxophone.
: That's right.
And, but you know --
How about the -- did you know Jerome Pasqual?

Oh, Jerome Pasqual. He was noted for very fine -- he was a very fine musician. He played a lot of clarinet and saxophone. He was one of the old pros that everybody looked up to around there. Was an excellent teacher, also. He taught very good saxophone.
Let's see, who else was playing -- oh! Delbert Bright.
: Del Bright!
Del Bright was playing an awful lot of saxophone --
: That's right.
-- back in those days, man. And, he was another cat was likened to Charlie Parker of his time.
Yeah, there's --
He was very fast and could play a lot of horn.
You have upset said a lot of those cats, I remember when you came in there. I was there.
I know. Dave Young played the good -- good tenor saxophone.
Right.
Dave Young was -- was a fine saxophone player. And, of course, (inaudible) you know at that time Ray Nance had a band that to me was just as great as John Kirby's Turbey's.
Right.
And, these guys, they double fiddled and they had -- oh, they had really, really, really a good band.
And, then, Jesse Simpkins. Poe.
Jesse Simpkins. Poe Simpkins on bass.
Yeah.
And --
Who was that little alto player? Harris? Was his name Harris?
Oh, Leroy Harris, who later joined Earl Hines' band. And --
: He played alto.

He played alto and he sang. He sang very good. In fact, he -- he -- he was the principal singer in Earl's band at one time, before Earl got, like, Billy Eckstine and Arthur D. Simpkins, and those guys. But, anyway, you know, it's a (inaudible) a good musicians.
: I just want to get -- now, you were there, and I was there, and I know you and I both have been for the second time. We might --
Oh, yeah.
-- 30-some years in our second marriage.
Well, see, I didn't marry till -- I'm getting close to my marriage now.
Oh, I see.
See? Cause after -- after the Louie Armstrong tour, then I came back and in 1934 Ruben Reeves organized a band.
Ruben Reeves was a trumpet player.
Trumpet player that used to be with Cab Calloway.
Right.
He had a brother named Gerald Reeves played trombone. Well, Ruben organized a band and he was

going to New York to work the Harlem Opera House. And, he needed a third trumpet. So, I told him I could play third trumpet. And, I had a trumpet. So, the music wasn't that hot, and I scuffled along third trumpet and then I doubled on tenor. I played all my solos on tenor. And, we came to New York and we played the -- no, it was the Alhambra Theater.
Alhambra, yeah.
We played the [Harlem Opera House] Alhambra Theater and -- and it -- you know whose show it was? It was W. C. Handy's show with J. Rosamond Johnson. And, we played the Alhambra.
What year was that, Budd?

This was in 1934. And, with Ruben Reeves band. So, after that job, after that job, we went -- we got out of New York, because we didn't have any more work. We went to Baltimore to work the Royal Theater. And, we -- we had an old manager out of Chicago. He had a hare lip, and he used to talk with a (inaudible), like that, you know. And, we all used to laugh at him, you know?
So, after we made our week at the -- at the Royal Theater in Baltimore --
Oh, yeah.
-- that's after we left New York. We went to the Royal Theater in Baltimore on Pennsylvania Avenue there.
Right.

And, after we made the first week, we -- we were getting ready to be paid off. And, there was a note in the pigeon hole for us. He says, "You laughed at my speech and everything, now, I got all of the money. Now, who's got the laugh last?" So, this cat had split with the whole payroll. Nobody got any money. So, now we are stranded in Baltimore.
So, we was sitting in Baltimpre stranded and I'm wondering what the heck am I gonna do. Nobody had no money, cause we didn't get no draw.
Right.

And, I'll tell you, Meil Young was on the piano in that band. And, so, McKinney's Cottonpickers came in town. And, Roy Eldridge and Joe Eldridge's brother and all of the cats in -- in -- what was the drummer's name? Cubie Austin?
Cubie Austin, right.
Well, Cubie was -- Cubie was -- was fronting the band. So, me and Roy used to get together and talk, so we used to go down to a place called the Moonglow. And, Ruben Blakely was the emcee there.
Ruben Blakely.
Ruben Blakely. And, and, the dancer, Baby -- Baby Lawrence, and another little partner of his. They were little kids. And, they were dancing in the show
there.
Now, this joint was a non-union joint. Excuse me.
Yeah, excuse me, but --
All right.
Yeah, go ahead. It was a non-union joint.

Yeah, so, as I say, this was a non-union joint, so Roy Eldridge said, "Come on, man, let's go down to the Moonglow and play some." So, Joe Eldridge, Roy Eldridge, and myself, Marl Young, would -- used to go down to this place and -- and blow. And, Joe would say -- tell the cat that owned the club, he said, "Hey, man, give those guys a quart of whiskey. Don't you see how hard they're working up there?"

And, sure enough, Joe would promote the whiskey, and we would get in there and just play for kicks. So, finally, Roy Eldridge said, "Hey, man," he says, "the people coming in here to hear us." Cause we would be going by there every night, you know. And, McKinney's Cottonpickers wasn't doing nothing. They were laying off.

So, he said, "Tell the man you want they job. Man, unionize this job, and you can get your gig and get to your grips." I said, "Hey, that's an idea." So, I said, "Okay, I'm going down to the union and I'm going to talk to the cats at the union," 'cause by this time my card wasn't paid up and

I'm sort of -- I'm on financial, too, you know, because I didn't have any money. And, I went down and talked to the guys in the union. I said, "Now, look, just give me permission to work here, and -- and I'll pay up my card. And, I'll get some money and at the same time I will have unionized a job," I said, because I just want to make enough money to get back to Chicago. Then, the guys in Baltimore has got some place to work. You know what I mean.

So, he says, "Yeah, that sounds good." So, they put me in good standing. And -- and paid for my card and give me a card and everything. And, sure enough, we talked the guy into giving us the job. Well, he didn't have to give the non-union man no notice, you know. And, at the same time, Ruben Blakely was very happy about this, because, you know, we were -- we were broke, see? And, this was -- this was beautiful.

Okay. So, we went in there and worked. Now, I'm the band leader. And, I'm getting $4.00 a night and I'm paying the men $2.00 a night. So, I get a room in that hotel right up over the place and I got a room in there for $5.00 a week. So, you can imagine how long I had to work there to save up enough money to get back to Chicago.
Anyway, May! Well Young asked for a raise. I said, "You got to be out of your mind, man. How am I going to pay you a raise then we -- I'm only getting four and you're

getting two, you know.

So, he says, "Well, man, I'm going to quit and go back to Chicago, then." I said, "Well, there's nothing I can do about it, you know." So, he left and went back to Chicago. The band started to sort of peter out, because I couldn't find too much talent around there. I used to go out to the race track with all them old rants tops, because they used to sit around and talk, and what not. And, they knew I was a little up against it, you see.

So, I came on went out to the track, you know, and bet a dollar, a couple dollars on this horse and the other". So, I'd make a little bet and win a little bit of money, you know, and like that, until finally I was able to go back to Chicago. But, I must have stayed in Baltimore about six months. Close to six months, getting that money together.

In the mean time, I had met this beautiful little girl in Chicago. Her name was Maimie Lawson. And, she was down at (Spellman) University doing the rest of it, going to school. Now, you know how Spellman got started, don't you?
No, how?
All of these -- well, the reason I know this story, cause her mother went to Spellman, also. And, --
Spellman College, that is.
Spellman College down in Georgia. And,
it was set up for these black kids who -- who were sired by rich white men by colored women. And, they -- mostly all of them were very fair. As you remember, my first wife.
Yes, she was beautiful.

And, well, she went to Spelman. So, I persuaded her after a year, let's get married. So, sure enough, in 1935, we got married. In the mean time, one day sitting at home I got this phone call from Ed Fox. Now --
Ed Fox.
-- Ed Fox was the manager of the Grand Terrace Cafe, and also for Earl Hines orchestra. I get this call. Kenny Stewart and myself.
Kenny Stewart was a trombone player, right?
Trombone player. Come up and join Earl's band at once. Had a fatal accident.
Oh, yeah.
And, this was May 10, 1935. I'll never forget the date. And, I was sorry about the accident, but very happy that I was going to join Earl Hines' band. I'd just married --
What happened to the accident?
Well, Cecil Irwin was killed out-right.
Right. Right.
He never knew what hit him. And, --
Billy Franklin?

Benny Franklin's arm, and everything was all messed up. Trommy's foot and leg -- Trommy Young was in the band. Omar Simian, glass had flew all in his face. They had picked it out. See what -- they were working at the Orpheum Theater in St. Paul, Minnesota. And, what happened -- I don't know whose fault it was. It must have been the other truck's fault. They hit this bus. Because Fox got a lot of money and he hardly gave those guys a dime of that money.

Anyway, when I got into the theater opening day for them, they were all sitting up bandaged on the stage playing. Can you imagine that? That's a thing about the show must go on. All of these guys were up there. They had lost Cecil Irving. He's dead. And, a couple of them were half dead. And, Billy Franklin can't play. He was -- because his arm was all crushed up and everything. And, the rest of the buys had bandages all over their heads and faces and arms, and feet and big legs, sitting up there playing the show. And, I -- I joined Earl Hines' band that night, Kenneth and myself.
Kenneth -- Kenneth Addison?
Kenneth Addison --
Right.
-- and myself. Well --
I remember that very well, Buddy.

We went on and Earl was paying me $7.00 a night. I think that was the average pay. I don't think nobody was making any more than that. $7.00 a night. So, anyway, we -- we came back to Chicago. But, before that, you know, before that I had been working in the Grand Terrace with Eddie Moore, the violin player, who had the band. Teddy Wilson with my brother, we still together. We're in the band. (Teddy Barnum) and all of these cats.
Trumpet players, yes.
Trumpet player. I was -- I was in the band. Guy Kelly.
Guy Kelly. Another trumpet player.
Yeah, and Preston Jackson.
Trombone.
Trombone.
Yeah.

Hey, these names are sort of coming back to me now. And, gee, who was -- oh, I'll think of some of these -- some of the other names. But, anyway, I started -- then, this is when I started the really try to write, because we had no music. And, I had -- I was making like one or two arrangements a day, and we'd come in and rehearse it. Because we had to go on the air. This was during the time Lindburgh's baby was kidnaped.
Is that right?

And, so, they broadcast all of this from the Grand Terrace. And, so, that made me do a lot of writing. So, I never will forget one time. A telephone -- a telegram came in and the telegram read like this, "Gee, Earl Hines, you sound beautiful on the piano. You certainly sound wonderful. I've really enjoyed you", you know. But, it was Teddy Wilson.
Well, see? A lot of people maybe don't know this, but Teddy Wilson lived with Earl Hines at one time when he first came round Chicago, and took piano lessons from Earl.
Wow.
He did some studying with Earl.
Great.
And, they used to play quite alike.
Yes.
And, then, of course, Tatum influence and everything, and then Teddy came into his own.
Sure.
But, I mean, --
Earl was quite influential for all piano players.
That's right. So, this guy thought it was Earl Hines playing. That's how great Teddy was playing then, you know. And, anyway, the band got some very fine

compliments and from this, also, I've got a telegram that the union called me over one day and they said we have a telegram from Prairie View College in Texas, and they want to know if you want to take the job as musical director.

I said, "Well, I'm really not qualified for that, you know, because I didn't have any degree in music or nothing like that. I'm just writing from the school of hard knocks, you know." And, anyway, so, then, after that, when Earl came back, and then went back out on the tour is when this accident happened. And, then, I joined the band.
And, then, of course, we came back in the Grand Terrace and there was a guy producing the shows named Percy Venable.
Right.

This was one of the greatest producers I've ever seen. What a mind he had. I didn't know this man was very heavy on dope at that time. But, you know, he would rehearse that show and rehearse that show and get it all together and until the last day when the show was about to open, we'd be rehearsing up until almost opening time. He would throw the finale together. And, it would be a classic. What a mind this cat had for shows. Percy Venable.
Well, I remember something about him. See if you can double check it. He had the longest fingernails of anybody I'd ever seen.
He seemed like he never cut his fingernails did he? And, he had this studio there over Wolgast's, you remember?
Right.
47 South Parkway. And, they used to do a lot of rehearsing up there. He had a big area up there. He was a very prominent man in the -- in the -- show producing.
In -- in black show business. One of the first great --

He was one of the greatest. That's right. So, anyway, we did shows, man, that you wouldn't believe. We used to do -- those girls used to dance to "Poet and Peasant", "Hunting the Black Forest", all of these classical pieces. And, we played this hard music and jazz and everything in these shows. They were great production numbers. I mean, just like Ziegfeld would put on or something, you know. With all of the costumes, with a big line of girls. But, those were the fun days, man.
That was a big -- Grand Terrace was the epitome of Chicago.
Well, it was --
-- (Inaudible) Chicago --
It was really something. I -- I never was in the Cotton Club, here in New York, I didn't get a chance to see that. But, if it had the Grand Terrace beat,

it had to go some, because I remember when people would be lined up all around the block to get in there, and they were paying $1.25 admission just to get in, a head. And, they would have standing room only, and people would be waiting for seats to see that show. That's how great it was. And, you know who the people would be? All the movie stars and rich, white businessmen.
You very seldom (Inaudible) saw a black couple in there.
That's right. I mean, it was just crammed and packed every night, man.
Where was the Grand Terrace located in, Budd?
That was on Oakwood Boulevard, which of course is South Parkway. And, what's that? 40th Street?
Oakwood Boulevard and South Parkway. Oakwood Boulevard was the boulevard --
Oakwood -- Oakwood Boulevard and South Parkway. Well, it was a -- this used to be an old Warner Brothers' theater.
Peerless Theater was the name of it when I was a kid.
Yeah.
Peerless Theater.
And, they made it into this nightclub.
Right.

And, of course, it was very convenient because all the artists would come that could stay upstairs at the Ritz Hotel, which was right on the corner, the drugstore underneath. They had everything right there.
The elevated came right by there.
That's right, and they went right by there.
Transportation.

The transportation was easy, and I never will forget. We had been down on one of our tours with Earl to Augusta, Georgia. And, we met this young man by the name of Arthur Lee Simpkins. And, we pursuaded him -- he was a good singer. So, we -- Earl wanted him to come to Chicago and to be with the band. So, he did.

We called him Georgia boy. And -- but, he was very intelligent. And, could sing. His name was Arthur Lee Simpkins. And, I never will forget one night. We're in there and Arthur Lee's singing in the band, and there's just -- all of a sudden this voice came out like from nowhere. 'There's my nigger.' And, when he said that, well, Bowman was the head waiter. And, these waiters went over and grabbed this cat and was really walking him. They were beating the hell out this man.
And, Arthur Lee was saying, 'No, no. Don't do that.

That's Mr. Finnegan. Don't do that. That's Mr. Finnegan." So, we said, "Who in the hell is Mr. Finnegan?" Well, he was the son of the president of one of the banks in Augusta, Georgia. And, Arthur Lee was trying to save him, you know what I mean?
Yeah. Yeah.

So, but they beat him so they had to take him away in an ambulance. And, I say that to say this. On one of our southern tours, we were to play Augusta. We bypassed it, baby. Earl says, "I'm not going into Augusta. Keep going." You know.

The interviewer shouldn't do too much interjection, but right here, just for the sake of your -- of your commentary here, I would like to let the listeners know about. We've mentioned this beautiful Grand Terrace and the clientele of it.
Yes.
Which was very high class and it was high class production.
Right.
I want to mention it was on what we call Grand Boulevard and Oakwood Boulevard. There --
That Grand Boulevard -- that's -- that's South Parkway now, but that's the original name, Grand Boulevard.
Yeah, that's what I just wanted to -- to -- so the people can understand.
That's right.
It was a -- it was a beautiful boulevard.
Oh, absolutely.
And, in those days, it was called Grand Boulevard, because in the days earlier than that, all those big mansions owned by the great meat packers, Armour and Swift --
Right.

-- had their big mansions on this boulevard. And, these were fantastic old houses and -- and they had begin to move out and go to Florida. But, these mansions were here on this boulevard. It was called Grand Boulevard.
Oh, I didn't know that.
Yeah. And, as black people begin to move in there, they thought the name Grand Boulevard was a little too high class for blacks. So, they named it South Parkway.
How about that?
They named it South Parkway.
That fits like a glove.
And, as times go on now, that same
boulevard is called Martin Luther King Boulevard. I just want to bring that in so that --
Isn't that -- that is quite a story.
So, that's how great it was and how great the Grand Terrace was.
Right. Right.
Please go on. I hope I didn't --

So, anyway, now, this band was going. Earl's band was very good. He always had a very good band. However, like in 19 -- well, 1937, we're sitting in the Grand Terrace playing. So, the waiter brought me a note and he said, "Here's a note for you, Budd. Now open it." He says, "This gentleman wants you to come over to his table and have a drink." Okay.

So, at intermission time, I went over to the table, sat down and had a drink. And he says, "Budd Johnson. Well, you don't know me." He says, "But, I met your mother in Dallas." Well, by this time, my mother, she was head maid at a very exclusive -- exclusive apartment building called Stony Court in Dallas.

And, he says, "I stayed at Stony Court, where your mother works. And, I was talking to her one day and told her that I was going to Chicago. She says, 'Oh, you are?' She says, 'Well, I have two boys that are musicians. One is with Cab Calloway and the other is working in the Grand
Terrace with Earl Hines.' And, he says, 'Yes, well, I'm going to Chicago.' And, he says, 'I'll go and see them.'"
So, he says, "So, let me introduce myself. My name is Gus Arnheim."
: Wow.

I said, "Gus Arnheim. Wow." Yeah, Bing Crosby was with him, and, you know, he had the -- he was a great band leader. He says, "She tells me you write music." I said, "Yes, I write it." He says, "Well, do the -- does Earl's band play any of your arrangements?" I said, "Yes." He said, "Well, would you have them to play one or two of them for me when you go back?" I said, "Certainly. I'd be delighted."

So, when I went back, I said, "Hey, Earl." I said, "I have a request to play a couple -- couple of things that I did in the band." Okay, no problem. So, we played them. And, when I went back to the table, he said, "Gee." He says, "I really like those arrangements." He says, "You think you would like to write for my band?" I said, "Sure. I wouldn't mind." He says, "Well, I mean, we're at the Congress Hotel now. We're going to be there for a month." He says, "We got a rehearsal tomorrow morning. Do you think you could have an arrangement ready by tomorrow morning?" I said, "I sure can."
And, I went home that night and wrote all night,
sat up all night and made up an original tune. I don't know what I called it. I -- I don't think I had a title for it.

Anyway, I was down to the Congress Hotel at 10:00 in the morning at this rehearsal. And, I passed the music out. Everybody like it. All the cats in the band liked it. And, he liked it. He said, "Well, would you like to go to join my band?" He says, "I tell you what." He says, "I can pay you $150 a week." And, he says, "And, your transportation."

I said, "Gee." I said, "That sounds good." I said, "But, I'm already working, you know. I'm with Earl Hines, man, you know, like I can't -- I just can't, you know, up and leave like that." I said. He says, "Well, you know, talk to him about it and see what happens."

So, sure enough, that night I spoke to Earl about it. I said, "I got a chance to go to this band and write it." "Gee," he says, "that sounds pretty good. Okay." He says, "You -- you can go." And, he says, "If it don't work out, you know, let me know, and you come on back."
Beautiful.

So, I joined Gus Arnheim's band as the arranger right there. Well, I noticed the piano player. He liked me and he kept, you know -- he says, "Come on up to the room and have dinner with me." And, he would have room service and we would eat steaks and what not. And, so, you know who
this piano was? Stan Kenton.
Oh!
Stan Kenton was the piano player in the band. And, he said, "Gee, I sure like -- I sure like the way you write right." He says, "Can you write some of them Earl things for me? The Earl Hines things."

-- and they would actually be fighting each other like -- they would be playing, but they would be hitting, trying to knock each other out and beat each other up, and when they got through, they would be wrecking the joint. A fourth part.
-- so I would have some music to play.

It's music, and basically it is that old music that we started to play, and maybe some call it -- they started off by saying ragtime and all of this stuff, but I mean you could take a guy that played a solo and put him behind a modern rhythm section, and it will still sound good, and it would fit.
Creative art form.

It's a creative art form, and it's original, and anything that's original I don't think like that -- in arts -- will ever die, and it's just going on and on. And I just hope that some of the youngsters can keep this thing going and find an interest in it. All right, so they like rock and roll, rock and roll. Okay, we used to like rock and roll. We put it down, and we tried to go on further. I see that they're even improving on that. And some of the stuff I hear today the kids are playing is very

great. They're playing better music. They're off of that one and two chord stuff. They're going on and on and on, and they're getting closer to the things we played, all the old solos, and the electronic things may be a little different. I think it'll be here forever.
Thank you. Hey, Budd, what are your hopes? You know what are your hopes? What do you wish is going to happen with it?

I wish that music should continue in the world forever, because if you ever stop to think if they shut off music, what would it be like? They tried that once when they had to stop the record band and all of this, and it was so bad and everything was silent, and you couldn't hear music, and people would get so depressed. But even sometimes when I get up and I feel a little bad and I turn my radio on, maybe I won't listen to jazz. I'll hear some beautiful string music and everything. I go to sleep with my radio on. Music is just a part of me. I hope that it will be a part of everyone in this country, whether he plays it, listens to it or enjoys seeing it or dancing to it or whatever. And I think it'll be here because music is as old as the world itself.
Music started out by the winds. Man tried to create the sounds of music by imitating the winds blowing through the trees, the waterfalls falling, making music. The
grunts and groans of the different beasts. That's music. And the birds that sing and everything.

Hey, Budd, I don't know how to thank you. In the words of your dear brother, Ray J Koo Johnson, which, when he finished one of his interviews with Perry Bradford, Kog said that he wished that all the world, all of the young people in the world could hear these stories and hear what the dues as you and people like you and people before us paid to get this beautiful art form to where it is, and that this is truly an American art form --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Copyright notice, Smithsonian header and Hinton's opening
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright notice, Smithsonian tape headers, sound check, and Milt Hinton introducing the March 5, 1975 interview with Budd Johnson.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: How Albert Johnson became "Budd"
segments.summary: Budd gives his full name and explains his uncle nicknamed him Butterbeans, later shortened to Budd.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Born in Dallas; brother saves him from a house fire
segments.summary: Born December 14, 1910; his four-year-old brother got him out of a burning house when he was two.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Parents and siblings
segments.summary: Names of his father and mother (Kate Estella Peak), the baby who died, brother Keg and sister Ruth Kathleen.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: His father's musical talent and church work
segments.summary: His self-educated father played trumpet and piano, turned down a circus job at his mother's insistence, led the choir at New Hope Baptist Church.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Piano lessons with Mr. Walton
segments.summary: Seven-year-old Budd learns piano by ear under a rap-on-the-knuckles teacher and quits when friends call pianists sissies.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Switching to drums; Dallas drummers and Alphonso Trent's band
segments.summary: Keg gets a trombone, Budd gets drums, admires Texas drummers and Alphonso Trent's sharp band, and becomes one of the best local drummers.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Snare drum at school and the first boyhood band
segments.summary: He drums for the marching lunch lines at school and forms a band with Keg and neighborhood friends.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Miss Puckett chaperones the boys' band on tours
segments.summary: A hip neighborhood lady books the child band into small Texas towns and settles pay back home with home brew and deductions.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Moonlight Melody Six and the Blue Moon Chasers
segments.summary: The band grows in high school, Budd teaches Booker Pittman alto, and the name changes to the Blue Moon Chasers.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Learning by copying records
segments.summary: The boys copy solos by Red Nichols, Hawkins, Henderson and Armstrong off records until they can hum and play them.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Ernest Williams offers a Tulsa roadhouse job
segments.summary: Southern Serenaders drummer Ernest Williams books the boys into a Tulsa road house; Budd explains road houses and his earlier Dallas job with Red Calhoun.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Stranded in Tulsa; TOBA show with Pigmeat Markham
segments.summary: The road house is padlocked, the boys live at the Greenwood Hotel and earn money ballyhooing for a TOBA show with Pigmeat Markham.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Sneaking out of the hotel and riding home to Dallas
segments.summary: Unable to pay, the boys lower their bags down a chute, escape at 3 a.m. in Lightnin's Packard, and Budd notes Keg stayed with him until Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Father the Studebaker mechanic
segments.summary: Budd's father worked for Studebaker from the wagon days, taught himself motors and became head of the Dallas parts department.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Segregation at the state fair and Juneteenth
segments.summary: Black visitors got only one day at the fair, called Juneteenth; Budd and Keg got in because their father demonstrated Studebakers.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Learning to drive and summer work at the Studebaker plant
segments.summary: His father kept his job through the Depression; Budd learned to drive delivering cars and earned good money unloading freight cars.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: Father's character, preaching and poll-tax exemption
segments.summary: Budd praises his father as a peacemaker, lay preacher and self-taught man who was exempt from the poll tax.

segments.chapter: Family and boyhood in Dallas
segments.title: His mother and Hinton's ties to the Johnson family
segments.summary: His mother sang beautifully but not in the choir and was a housewife; Hinton recalls knowing her and staying with her friend in Dallas.

segments.chapter: Teenage tours and Ben Webster
segments.title: Phone interruption and resuming the tape
segments.summary: A phone call interrupts the tape; they resume with the Tulsa story.

segments.chapter: Teenage tours and Ben Webster
segments.title: Correcting Chilton's Who's Who; the Sammy Price audition
segments.summary: Budd sets the record straight that Sammy Price did not organize the Blue Moon Chasers, who auditioned and rejected him.

segments.chapter: Teenage tours and Ben Webster
segments.title: Stranded in Oklahoma City and Guthrie under Mr. Brown
segments.summary: A chaperoned tour pays 25 cents a man in Guthrie, and the boys survive on cabbages and watermelons taken from fields.

segments.chapter: Teenage tours and Ben Webster
segments.title: Southern Serenaders in Oklahoma City: Hot Lips Page, Rushing and Walter Page
segments.summary: The band that rescues the boys includes Hot Lips Page, Bill Owens, Walter Page, Jimmy Rushing, and young Charlie Christian.

segments.chapter: Teenage tours and Ben Webster
segments.title: When Budd first met Charlie Christian
segments.summary: Hinton and Budd sort out the date of Budd's first meeting with Charlie Christian, before John Hammond discovered him.

segments.chapter: Teenage tours and Ben Webster
segments.title: Battle of music at Slaughter's Hall
segments.summary: The Southern Serenaders stage a benefit battle of music so the stranded boys can go home.

segments.chapter: Teenage tours and Ben Webster
segments.title: Joining Eugene Coy's Happy Black Aces and the trip to Amarillo
segments.summary: After graduating in 1928, Budd and Keg join Eugene Coy in Shawnee, whose job ends and band drives through blowouts to Amarillo.

segments.chapter: Teenage tours and Ben Webster
segments.title: Meeting Ben Webster in Amarillo and teaching him sax
segments.summary: Ben Webster is playing piano for silent films; Budd shows him the saxophone and Trumbauer's Singing the Blues.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Call from T. H. Smith to the first Black nightclub in Dallas
segments.summary: T. H. Smith, a real-estate man, calls the Johnsons home to join the band at the new North Dallas Club.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Jesse Stone auditions the Dallas musicians
segments.summary: Jesse Stone, hired as musical director, gives each local musician a reading test at Arthur Alexander's house.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: T. Holder and the two Twelve Clouds of Joy
segments.summary: Bandleader T. Holder had run off with the original Twelve Clouds of Joy's money, so Andy Kirk got that band while Holder used the name again in Dallas.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Booker Pittman's family and Booker T. Washington connection
segments.summary: Booker Pittman's family in Dallas: his mother Portia taught music at the high school, his father was a contractor.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: The Taliaferro name and Booker T. Washington's work with Indians
segments.summary: Budd guesses how the Washington family acquired Indian-sounding names after reading a book on Washington.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Jane Pittman question; Booker's cruel father
segments.summary: Hinton asks about Miss Jane Pittman; Budd describes Pittman senior as a scandal-sheet publisher who beat his son.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: T. Holder strands the band; Jesse Stone takes over
segments.summary: T. Holder absconds with the money again in Oklahoma, so the band makes Jesse Stone leader and becomes the Blue Serenaders in St. Joseph.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: St. Joseph, Missouri: Stone's background and Coleman Hawkins
segments.summary: Blue Serenaders was Coleman Hawkins's first band; Stone came from Atchison, Kansas; fourteen men crowd two rooms in the Charlotte Hotel.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Rehearsing in St. Joseph; George E. Lee hears the band
segments.summary: The stranded band rehearses daily; George E. Lee hears them at the Frog Hop Ballroom and is scared by their arrangements.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Jesse Stone teaches Budd to write; "Idaho" and "W.P.A."
segments.summary: Stone inspired Budd's writing; Budd describes Stone's hits and the Congressional investigation of "W.P.A.", and his later career.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Lineup of the Blue Serenaders
segments.summary: Hinton and Budd list the band's members: Tompkins, Keg, Durham, violinist Claude, Booker Pittman and John R. Davis.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Working for tips at a roadhouse in Dallas, Missouri
segments.summary: The band takes a no-salary job outside Kansas City, pools tips in a kitty and visits Kansas City on weekends.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Southern Serenaders become Walter Page's Blue Devils
segments.summary: Budd clarifies that the Southern Serenaders of 1927 became Walter Page's Blue Devils and later Basie's band.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: Dice game with the boss; the apartment at 13th and Lydia
segments.summary: Stone wins the boss's money, the band is fired and moves to an apartment at 13th and Lydia in Kansas City.

segments.chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
segments.title: First Kansas City band with written music
segments.summary: Jesse Stone's Blue Serenaders were the only band with written arrangements, with better harmony than Bennie Moten.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Sleeping in Paseo Park and Street's Poolhall
segments.summary: Stranded again, the musicians sleep in the park and use Street's Poolhall as an address, while Budd hides his plight from his father.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Meeting Count Basie at the Eblon Theater
segments.summary: Budd jams in the pit with Basie, who plays for silent pictures at the Eblon.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Keg goes to Minneapolis; Lester Young arrives with the Blue Devils
segments.summary: Keg writes about a sax player named Lester Young; the Blue Devils come to Kansas City with Lester, whom Budd compares to Trumbauer.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Lester upsets Kansas City; Budd gives him his first reefer
segments.summary: Lester Young is wowing Kansas City musicians, and Budd and Prez become friends.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Booker T. Washington Hotel, Elnora's restaurant and Maceo Pinkard
segments.summary: Hinton and Budd recall the Eblon, hotel, Street's and Elnora's restaurant, and Pinkard's drugstore.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Hanging out with Prez in Kansas City
segments.summary: Budd and Prez gather in the hotel lobby, and Prez wakes him at night to cut visiting tenor players.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Ben Webster takes Budd's place and returns to Kansas City
segments.summary: Ben replaced Budd with Eugene Coy, outplayed him when Budd was with George E. Lee, and came home to Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Jap Allen's band and Clyde Hart's arrangements
segments.summary: Ben joins Jap Allen's band, with Clyde Hart writing arrangements amid McKinney's Cotton Pickers' fame.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Straightening out the 1929-30 chronology
segments.summary: Hinton and Budd pin down which year they are discussing.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Taking George E. Lee's chair in Kansas City
segments.summary: After Stone's band breaks up, Budd sits in George E. Lee's chair, gets the job, and notes he reached Chicago January 9, 1932.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Jap Allen vs. McKinney's Cotton Pickers battle of bands
segments.summary: Booker and Ben join Jap Allen, and McKinney's men accuse Allen of stealing arrangements Clyde Hart transcribed from records.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Booker and Ben go with Blanche Calloway; Booker to Europe
segments.summary: Pittman and Webster join Blanche Calloway, and Booker later goes to Europe and South America.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Bill Pemberton joins the interview; the JPJ Quartet
segments.summary: Hinton welcomes Bill Pemberton, who works with Budd in the JPJ Quartet.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Booker Pittman's lost six years in South America
segments.summary: Booker tells Budd he lost six years cutting cane in South America in a daze before recovering and becoming a star bandleader.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Seeing Booker in Brazil shortly before his death
segments.summary: Budd records with Booker in New York, then visits him in Brazil in about 1966-67 when Booker is dying of throat cancer.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
segments.title: Hinton and Pemberton on Booker's disappearance
segments.summary: Hinton confirms musicians in South America talked about Booker, and Pemberton asks where in Brazil he was.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Moving to Chicago in January 1932 to join Keg
segments.summary: Hinton steers Budd back to his own story; Keg writes from Chicago that musicians there are prosperous, and Budd, who wanted to play with Earl Hines, arrives January 9, 1932.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: First Chicago band: Ed Cary, Guy Kelly and the Cary family
segments.summary: Budd recalls his first Chicago band under Ed Cary and its members while Hinton adds that Scoops Cary was his classmate.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Rehearsing with Milt Hinton; Tick Gray's roadhouse group
segments.summary: Budd and Hinton rehearse daily and play a roadhouse with Tick Gray; Hinton's mother refuses to let him go to Milwaukee.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Bill Winston's basement hangout and the Chicago musicians' scene
segments.summary: Musicians gather in Bill Winston's basement, recall drummers and the Cobb brothers who carried pistols, and local union politics.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: The Villa Venice band lineup
segments.summary: Budd names the men in the Villa Venice band with Keg, Eddie Mallory and others.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Petrillo's threat and the Villa Venice show
segments.summary: On opening night Petrillo threatens to run the Black band off, Budd describes the grand Villa Venice with gondolas, and how they transposed foreign acts' music.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Sixty dollars a week and escorts through Capone territory
segments.summary: The owner keeps the band at $60 and has armed men drive them through Capone's territory; later Teddy Wilson's car runs the north side.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Floyd Campbell's combo at the Panama on 58th Street
segments.summary: Floyd Campbell hires Budd for the Panama on "Dodge City" 58th Street, with Gideon Honore and Jabo Smith.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Jabo Smith and the Jenkins Orphanage Band
segments.summary: Budd describes Jabo Smith's trumpet and trombone talent, and the orphanage band that marched to raise funds.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: How Budd got the Panama job from Henry Allen
segments.summary: Henry Allen passed the Floyd Campbell job to Budd; the band was very good, shortly before joining Louis Armstrong in late 1932.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Irene Eddy and Teddy Wilson at Mrs. Otter's house
segments.summary: Budd and Teddy Wilson boarded at Mrs. Otter's on South Parkway, where Wilson rehearsed hours daily and showed Budd 'Liza' runs.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Joining Louis Armstrong's band: lineup and rehearsal
segments.summary: Armstrong sends for Budd via Mac McKendrick; Budd lists Z. T. Randolph, Stump Evans, Keg, the Oldham brothers, Teddy Wilson and Yank Porter.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: A white fan says "you're not like the others" in San Antonio
segments.summary: A white man tells the Armstrong band members they are different from "niggers" in town, and Budd reflects on where the band's members came from.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Forty dollars pro rata and Cincinnati
segments.summary: The Armstrong band learns the $40 weekly pay was pro rata and stops getting paid full wages in Cincinnati.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Armstrong's contract with Collins and Rockwell
segments.summary: Budd explains how Armstrong's lawyer Collins held power of attorney and obliged him to pay Rockwell $150 a week after his California reefer arrest.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: The band strikes at Castle Farms in Cincinnati
segments.summary: The musicians refuse to play until paid the full $40, Armstrong waits alone at Castle Farms, then the band breaks up back in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
segments.title: Armstrong splits from Collins and teams up with Joe Glaser
segments.summary: Armstrong learns the cost of power of attorney, tells Budd he will go with Glaser who is leaving prison, and Glaser builds an empire.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Tape Three headers
segments.summary: Smithsonian headers for the new tape.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Ed Fox feud; Budd and Eckstine reorganize Earl Hines's band
segments.summary: Budd tells Hines to rebuild the band while Fox's clique left, with himself as musical director and deposits locked in the Ritz Hotel safe.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Recruiting the new Hines band
segments.summary: Budd and Billy Eckstine hire Truck Parham, Hurley Ramey, Scoops Cary, trumpeters and trombonists for the new Hines band.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Bob Red Cross's room and rehearsing at the Chicago union hall
segments.summary: Musicians walk daily from the Michigan Hotel to the union hall, where Tubby Hall cooks red beans and rice, and Budd mentions a photo of Ben Webster.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Outwitting Ed Fox on the first job
segments.summary: The band memorizes its book and hides the music at the Ritz, so Fox's police find no music to confiscate at the first dance.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: First tour, personnel and the 1938-39 band
segments.summary: Budd names Robert Crowder, Franz Jackson and the arrangement 'Yellow Five', and calls this one of Hines's best bands.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Western tour: Jim Crow hotels, John Williams cooking and bus trouble
segments.summary: On a 1940 tour through Montana, Utah and Idaho the band stays in Chinese hotels and cooks its own food, and the bus fails in the mountains.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Oakland, Club Plantation and Ellington's Jump for Joy
segments.summary: The Hines band plays Sweet's Ballroom and a Los Angeles club while Ellington's Jump for Joy is in town.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Band pay scale and managing Hines's business
segments.summary: Budd and Eckstine set the band's pay, pay Hines $15 a night, and put Charlie Carpenter in the William Morris office to plan bus routes.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Pay dispute with Hines
segments.summary: Eckstine gets a raise to $25 a night, Hines refuses Budd the same, and Budd announces he is quitting in December 1942.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Recording in Los Angeles: 'Jelly, Jelly' and 'Boogie Woogie on the St. Louis Blues'
segments.summary: Back in 1941 the band records in L.A.; Budd says the arrangements were his, with Eckstine writing lyrics.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: A night with Nat King Cole and brother Eddie Cole
segments.summary: Budd sits in at a Hollywood party with Cole's trio and recalls Nat and Eddie Cole struggling in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Rebuilding the Earl Hines band, 1938-42
segments.title: Leaving Hines and returning to New York
segments.summary: After a second California tour in 1941, Budd quits Hines in December 1942, goes through Dallas and joins his second wife Bernice in New York.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: The Moonglow on 52nd Street; Don Byas hands Budd his job
segments.summary: Budd sits in with Dizzy Gillespie, Byas, Max Roach and Pettiford at the Moonglow, and Byas, leaving for Ellington, offers him the job.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Learning the new bebop tunes with Dizzy and Pettiford
segments.summary: Budd finds the bop repertoire difficult, writes down Pettiford's tunes, and sees this as a new trend.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: How bebop got its name
segments.summary: Budd's theory that the name came from Dizzy humming phrases to explain them.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Coleman Hawkins's bebop-era record date
segments.summary: Hawkins organizes a session with Dizzy, Clyde Hart and Howard McGhee; Budd arranges 'De Dakt' and Dizzy 'Woody 'n' You'.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Byas misses Ellington; the Moonglow band splits
segments.summary: Byas does not get the Ellington job, and Budd stays while Pettiford starts his own group.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Yacht Club with Dizzy; record men hustling on 52nd Street
segments.summary: Budd manages Dizzy's group at the Yacht Club while Timmy Rosenkrantz and others hunt for musicians to record, and Django sits in at the Three Deuces.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Hawkins and Monk's tunes; first bop recordings
segments.summary: Hawkins was crazy about Monk, and the date he organizes yields among the first bop records.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Pirated recordings and uncollected royalties
segments.summary: Hinton and Budd discuss wire-recorded party tapings sold in Europe and royalties musicians never knew to collect.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Collectors, party tapings and V-Discs
segments.summary: Budd describes a Chicago collector selling air shots and the V-Discs from the war sold as limited collector's editions.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Copyrights taken by smarter men on the Street
segments.summary: Musicians who never knew about copyright lost their tunes to opportunists like arranger Walter Fuller.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: The White Rose bar; Coleman Hawkins as "the Bean"
segments.summary: Budd explains Hawkins's nickname and says Hawkins attended the University of Kansas and never revealed his age.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Lionel Hampton's record date with Spencer Odom
segments.summary: Budd and Spencer Odom write arrangements for Hamp's record date in Chicago while Benny Goodman is in town.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Jerry Jerome at the White Rose offers an NBC arranging job
segments.summary: Jerry Jerome recognizes Budd in the bar and hires him as staff arranger at NBC in late 1943.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Learning to write for the Hammond organ at NBC
segments.summary: Given an odd instrumentation including Hammond organ, Budd buys an organ book and crams to write the parts.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Four arrangements in two days; NBC wants him slowed down
segments.summary: Budd condenses Fred Waring scores into small-band arrangements so fast that management objects.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Wanting to leave NBC; summoned by the conductor
segments.summary: Budd does not want to be a writing machine and is called in by Jerry Jerome before a break in the taping.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: The organist praises Budd's organ parts
segments.summary: The organist asks to study with Budd because of his careful registration stops, though Budd never attended a rehearsal.

segments.chapter: New York, bebop and NBC
segments.title: Begging out of the NBC contract
segments.summary: Budd asks to be released from his union contract because he wants to play, against his wife's wishes.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: Bands and singers Budd has arranged for
segments.summary: At Hinton's request Budd lists the leaders he has written for, from Hines to Ivory Joe Hunter's 'I Almost Lost My Mind'.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: Stock arrangements for Benny Goodman's sextet
segments.summary: Budd wrote stock arrangements of Goodman sextet tunes such as 'Soft Winds', a solo for Charlie Christian.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: Other writing: Goodman, Harry James, Basie and the Jazz Repertory Company
segments.summary: Budd names more bandleaders, his year and a half with Goodman, the New York Jazz Repertory Company and his 1961 Basie stint.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: The JPJ Quartet
segments.summary: Budd, Oliver Jackson and Bill Pemberton formed the quartet in 1969, played for Johns-Manville, then Yugoslavia and Montreal in 1971.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: Studying orchestration with Hale Smith for a youth symphony piece
segments.summary: Budd takes on a Kennedy Center commission and learns orchestration from Hale Smith and Piston's book.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: Tunes for Woody Herman, Georgie Auld and Gene Krupa
segments.summary: Budd wrote 'Concerto for Tenor' for Georgie Auld, an arrangement of Redman's 'Cherry' for Herman, and 'What's This' for Krupa.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: Writing for Ina Ray Hutton and Boyd Raeburn; Jimmy Noone's influence
segments.summary: Budd and Dizzy write for Ina Ray Hutton and Raeburn, and Budd says Benny Goodman's clarinet sound derives from Jimmy Noone, for whom Budd wrote.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: Armstrong arrangements and George E. Lee: Budd learns to write
segments.summary: Budd wrote arrangements for Armstrong's 1933 records and early charts for George E. Lee, borrowing standards' changes.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: New melodies on standard chord changes
segments.summary: Hinton and Budd explain that boppers wrote new lines over standard changes because a chord progression cannot be copyrighted.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: "Grooving High" and "How High the Moon"; Benny Harris and Garner
segments.summary: Budd demonstrates how 'Grooving High' was built on 'How High the Moon' and 'Whispering', and mentions Erroll Garner and 'Misty'.

segments.chapter: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
segments.title: Atlantic Records, Ruth Brown and Sarah Vaughan dates
segments.summary: Budd was musical director at Atlantic, wrote 'Teardrops from My Eyes' for Ruth Brown, and arranged a date when Sarah Vaughan's arranger failed.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Tape Four headers
segments.summary: Smithsonian headers for the next tape.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Zilner Randolph's impossible arrangements
segments.summary: Z. T. Randolph wrote arrangements full of 64th notes to stump the band, such as 'Body and Soul'.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Stump Whitlock plays Louis's "Shine"
segments.summary: Budd corrects himself that Ellis "Stump" Whitlock, not Stump Evans, was the trumpeter Louis let play 'Shine', including in Louisville.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Naming the Armstrong band
segments.summary: Budd and Hinton list the personnel of Armstrong's 1933 band, including Scoville Brown, Oldham brothers, Wilson, Yank Porter and McKendrick.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: "Laughing Louie" and "Sweet Sue" in the vipers' language
segments.summary: The band smokes before recording 'Laughing Louie', and Budd sings a chorus of 'Sweet Sue' in their made-up viper language.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Visiting the dying Freddie Keppard with Armstrong
segments.summary: On the first trip out of Chicago, Armstrong has the bus driver take the band to see Keppard, who died a week later.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: The St. Louis Vipers Club's giant joint
segments.summary: A St. Louis vipers club presents Armstrong with a baseball-bat-sized joint, and police guard the band's dressing room while they smoke.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Armstrong's 250 high C's against Hal Baker
segments.summary: Armstrong answers an imitation of 'Shine' by Hal Baker with 250 high C's; in Oklahoma City the band plays blind high on pot.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Armstrong's repertoire in 1933
segments.summary: Budd lists the old tunes Louis played with the band, such as 'Ding Dong Daddy' and 'High Society'.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Albert system versus Boehm clarinets
segments.summary: Hinton and Budd discuss the old Albert system clarinet and who still plays it, with Buster Bailey a favorite.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Chicago saxophonists of the early 1930s
segments.summary: Budd names Leon Washington, Boyd Atkins, Omer Simeon, Cecil Irvin and Doll Hutchison in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Scoops Cary, Del Bright and other Chicago players
segments.summary: Budd likens Scoops Cary and Del Bright to Charlie Parker and recalls Jerome Pasquall, Dave Young, Ray Nance's band and Leroy Harris.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: The Ruben Reeves band at the Alhambra, 1934
segments.summary: Budd plays third trumpet and tenor with Reeves's band for W. C. Handy's show at the Alhambra in New York.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Stranded in Baltimore after the manager runs off
segments.summary: At the Royal Theater the band's manager disappears with the payroll and leaves the musicians stranded.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Unionizing the Moonglow job in Baltimore with Roy Eldridge
segments.summary: Budd and Roy Eldridge jam at a non-union club, and Budd gets his union card paid and takes over the job as leader.

segments.chapter: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
segments.title: Marl Young leaves; Budd saves money at the race track
segments.summary: Pianist Marl Young quits over a raise, and Budd bets at the track to earn the fare back to Chicago, thinking of Mamie Lawson.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Courting and marrying Mamie Lawson of Spelman College
segments.summary: Budd tells how Spelman was founded for fair-skinned children of white fathers, and how he persuaded his first wife to marry him in 1935.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Joining Earl Hines after the bus accident, May 1935
segments.summary: Ed Fox calls Budd and Kenneth Addison to replace casualties of a bus crash in St. Paul, and Budd joins the bandaged band that night.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: The Grand Terrace broadcasts, Teddy Wilson's telegram and Prairie View offer
segments.summary: Writing one or two arrangements a day for Eddie Moore's radio band, Budd gets a fan telegram that was really from Teddy Wilson, and a job offer from Prairie View College.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Percy Venable's Grand Terrace shows
segments.summary: Budd praises show producer Percy Venable and the elaborate productions with classical pieces and a line of girls.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: The Grand Terrace: crowds, clientele and location
segments.summary: Budd describes the club's lines around the block, white audience, and the former Peerless theater on Oakwood and South Parkway.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Arthur Lee Simpkins and the beating of Mr. Finnegan
segments.summary: Singer Arthur Lee Simpkins tried to protect a banker's son whom waiters beat after he called out a slur, so Earl bypassed Augusta.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: How Grand Boulevard became South Parkway
segments.summary: Hinton explains the boulevard was named for the meat packers' mansions and renamed South Parkway as Black families moved in.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Gus Arnheim offers Budd an arranging job
segments.summary: Arnheim, who met Budd's mother in Dallas, hears Budd's charts at the Grand Terrace and hires him for $150 a week with Hines's blessing.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Stan Kenton asks for Earl Hines-style charts
segments.summary: Pianist Stan Kenton befriends Budd in Arnheim's band and asks for arrangements in Earl Hines's manner.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Arnheim's band in Minneapolis and New York with Jimmy Mundy
segments.summary: Budd drives to Minneapolis and then the Hotel New Yorker, writes four arrangements weekly, and Arnheim backs his authority as musical director.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Joe Dixon, Lou Singer and the end of Arnheim's band
segments.summary: Arnheim names his chums and then breaks up the band to take a California bank job.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Playing with Horace Henderson before rejoining Hines
segments.summary: Back in Chicago Budd plays at the Savoy with Horace Henderson, a great arranger now raising horses in Colorado.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Meeting Billy Eckstine in Washington and Detroit
segments.summary: Budd urges singer Billy Eckstine to come to Chicago and shares his Detroit hotel room.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Eckstine at Club DeLisa; "you can't quit" the mob
segments.summary: Fox rejects Eckstine, who takes a job at Mike DeLisa's, where Budd says nobody was allowed to quit and Scatman Crothers was beaten for leaving.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Writing for Billy Eckstine with Earl Hines
segments.summary: Budd writes Eckstine's vocal charts, including 'I Love the Rhythm in a Riff' and 'Water Boy', while Hines pays little per chart.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: "You Don't Know What Love Is" at the North Dallas Club
segments.summary: Eckstine's slow ballad at a Dallas dance leads to a ruckus as dancers hold each other tightly.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Cliques in the Hines band
segments.summary: Factions divide the band as Hines and Fox feud, and Budd lists the trumpets and trombones.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Tape Five headers
segments.summary: Smithsonian headers for Tape Five.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: Fort Lauderdale 1938: segregated laws and armed musicians
segments.summary: Hinton asks for the Earl Hines story; police keep white women away from the bandstand and the band carries guns.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: A drunk demands "Honeysuckle Rose"
segments.summary: After the flag-waver a drunk insults Hines, who answers sharply, while Budd unlatches his brother's pistol in the briefcase.

segments.chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
segments.title: The state trooper and Earl Hines hiding in the bus
segments.summary: A trooper takes the drunk's side until a white Hollywood fan intervenes, and Hines escapes to hide among the clothes in the bus.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Joining Cab Calloway's band in 1947
segments.summary: Budd joins Calloway in Chattanooga replacing Rudy Powell, praises the organization, and gets a pink slip at the Capitol Theater.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Issa El Saieh invites Budd to Haiti
segments.summary: Issa El Saieh takes lessons from Budd and offers him a round trip, $200 a week and $100 for his wife to teach Haitian musicians.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Who Issa El Saieh was
segments.summary: Budd describes El Saieh's Arab and Lebanese family background, the family business and his art dealing.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Recording the Haitian drummers in New York
segments.summary: Budd arranges a record date with Ti-Roro and other Haitian drummers, Hilton Jefferson, Hinton and Pemberton.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Lost records and meeting Issa El Saieh again at Montreux
segments.summary: Budd's stored records mildewed, and in 1971 he runs into El Saieh and his son at Montreux.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Five years teaching in Haiti, the Billy Taylor Quartet and Marian Anderson
segments.summary: Budd returns to Haiti yearly, brings the Billy Taylor quartet to the centennial fair, and plays for a colonel at the palace.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Circular breathing makes Haitian headlines
segments.summary: Budd's five-minute held note astonishes Haitians, and he explains circular breathing, as Clark Terry and Buster Bailey also did.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Discovering Sarah Vaughan at the Apollo amateur night
segments.summary: Billy Eckstine and Budd persuade Earl Hines to hire a shabby young Sarah Vaughan after hearing her at the Apollo, and Hines buys her dresses.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Writing for Sarah Vaughan; two pianos; Jerry Valentine
segments.summary: Hines stages Vaughan at a second piano, Budd becomes her chief arranger alongside Jerry Valentine.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: Eckstine and Vaughan duets; the Three Varieties with Madeline Green
segments.summary: Budd, Willie Randall and Leroy Harris sing backing as the Three Varieties behind Madeline Green; Budd says Green and Randall had a son.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
segments.title: First marriage, a miscarriage, and sons born three days apart
segments.summary: Budd's first wife lost a child, and after both remarried they each had sons days apart; they stay good friends.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Hilton Jefferson: drinking buddy, Cab's punishing feature numbers
segments.summary: Hinton asks Budd about colleagues, and Budd praises Hilton Jefferson, whom Cab would test with hard features when he was drunk.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Chu Berry and Roy Eldridge
segments.summary: Budd recalls meeting Chu Berry in Chicago, describes his Hawkins-derived style, and Roy Eldridge's love of Hawkins and Armstrong records.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Benny Carter, "the King"
segments.summary: Budd rates Benny Carter among the greatest altos and tells a story of Phil Harris saying Carter scored his wife's films and played parts for the men.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Meeting Charlie Parker at 55th and Michigan in Chicago
segments.summary: Parker, hoboing into Chicago, blows with Goon Gardner's group and reminds Budd he used to peek into George E. Lee's rehearsals as a Kansas City boy.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Parker in New York; buying Tadd Dameron's first arrangement
segments.summary: Parker, Monk and Dameron visit Budd's home, and the Hines sax section's mistake fines pay for Dameron's 'Sweet Georgia Brown'.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Bob Carroll and the fake fights of New York tenor players
segments.summary: Budd recalls tenor Bob Carroll, who staged fake bar fights with Ben Webster and others and was ruined by drink.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Russell Procope and joining John Kirby's band in 1944
segments.summary: Charlie Shavers recommends Budd to replace Buster Bailey with Kirby in Baltimore, where he plays the seventh chair on tenor without music.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Prince Robinson
segments.summary: Budd praises Prince Robinson as nearly equal to Hawkins and recalls Clyde Hart copying his solo on 'Zonky'.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Why and when Budd took up the soprano saxophone
segments.summary: Hinton praises Budd's in-tune soprano; Budd explains the horn's history and that his wife persuaded him to switch from clarinet.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Understudying Sidney Bechet in "Hear That Music"
segments.summary: Budd is hired on 48th Street as Bechet's understudy for a short-lived play that opens and closes within a week.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: The future of jazz
segments.summary: Budd compares jazz to the airplane, a foundation that keeps growing, and approves of young players moving beyond one-chord rock.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Why music will always continue
segments.summary: Budd hopes music will be part of everyone's life and explains that it began with imitations of nature.

segments.chapter: Colleagues and reflections
segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Hinton thanks Budd, citing Keg Johnson's wish that young people hear these stories.
